# CHAPTER 402

## THE SHOPPER

Westbank had a market.

This was dangerous.

Not because of thieves.

Probably.

Because Mella Torr mentioned it while I was eating my second potato.

"Boat yard row sets tables after noon," she said. "Mostly hooks, cord, smoked things, old river junk. Since the second sun started, everyone's selling anything shiny for twice what it's worth."

I stopped chewing.

"Finish lunch before you shop."

"I haven't said anything."

"Temporary condition."

"Mella."

"What?"

"He looked sad."

Probably.

He folded it again.

Sori compared five mornings of timing.

Less biting.

Mostly.

I walked Westbank slowly.

Boat repair sheds had hulls upside down on blocks.

Children scraped old pitch from planks for coins.

A woman smoked tiny silver fish over alder wood.

Two men argued whether a boat named **MOTHER'S PATIENCE** had ever possessed either.

A shrine near upstream dock held river stones stacked in pairs.

No one explained it.

I didn't ask.

The Two Suns had already added a second painted yellow disk beside old heron sign.

Badly.

Mella was delighted.

"Tourists like bad paint. Feels authentic."

"Authentic to what?"

"Paying me."

Respect.

Late afternoon, messenger arrived from White Span.

Not emergency.

Lessa.

She walked in carrying a board and immediately stole bread from our table.

"Fenner says tomorrow's surface won't be as calm. North wind expected before dawn."

Dask sat up.

"How strong?"

"Enough to make little chop. Not enough to close ferry."

There.

New variable.

Vessa said, "Does local request still want observation?"

"More. Fenner says if wrong light needs calm water, maybe tomorrow tells us something."

Dask looked almost happy.

Lessa pointed bread at him.

"Don't."

He controlled face.

"I am not doing anything."

"You're thinking loudly."

Sori pulled clean sheet.

"Expected wind direction?"

"North to northeast. Starts weak before dawn, strengthens around sunrise if weather office isn't lying."

Maro said, "River runs east-southeast there."

Lessa nodded.

"So cross-ripple."

Greg brain moved.

Not locked.

Just interested.

If phenomenon required mirror-like surface, chop should break it.

If it appeared anyway and followed each small face of water, different evidence.

If it appeared only in sheltered patches behind piers, useful.

If nothing appeared, still useful but not proof.

One morning absence meant one morning absence.

Dask said, "We should establish chop before first light."

"Yes," Vessa said.

"And compare sheltered water under west bank."

"Ask Fenner."

"And perhaps place a controlled flat pan adjacent to river surface to test sky geometry without river continuity."

That was actually good.

I looked at him.

"That's better than bucket after."

He looked pleased.

"Yes."

Sori said, "Don't encourage him."

Lessa swallowed bread.

"Fenner has wash basin."

"Clean?" Dask asked.

"No."

"Can it be cleaned?"

"Probably."

"Material?"

"Metal."

"Reflective?"

"It's a basin, Dask."

"That does not answer."

"Then come look at stupid basin."

He did.

Of course.

Vessa sent Maro too.

I stayed.

That was growth.

Or shoulder.

Both.

Evening came slow over Lume.

From Westbank, physical sunset happened west like respectable celestial behavior.

No second sun.

No wrong reflection.

Just orange river and smoke.

I sat on inn step with new slate plate in lap.

Thirteen copper now.

Vale twenty-three.

Quietener eight.

Plate one.

Bath one.

Money moving.

Not disappearing.

Becoming things.

Some temporary.

Hot water.

Some durable.

Tools.

Some future obligation.

Vale.

That distinction mattered more than purse number.

First life, eventually, I had enough money that small purchases stopped being decisions.

I had thought that was freedom.

It was.

Also made it easier to accumulate stupid shit.

Second life had taught me something poverty had not.

Not **never spend**.

That was fear.

Spend where object changed options.

The quietener did.

Maybe.

The slate plate did in smaller way.

Hot bath changed one evening and next morning's shoulder.

Also worth money.

Different durations.

Different value.

Sori came outside.

"You're counting."

"Thinking."

"Same face."

"Thirteen."

"I know."

"Stop knowing my money."

"You announce purchases like military victories."

"One copper."

"Historic."

I held plate up.

"Useful."

"Probably."

"Rude."

She sat beside me.

For a while we watched river.

Then she said, "You know tomorrow might show nothing."

"Yes."

"Dask will be unbearable."

"Yes."

"Fenner will look personally betrayed by water."

"Probably."

"You?"

I thought.

"Write nothing."

She nodded.

"Good."

That was witness job.

But shopper job had been better.

More immediate.

Pay copper.

Get thing.

Cause and effect.

Beautiful.

River did not respect commerce.

Before bed, Vessa gathered us for ten minutes.

Tomorrow plan changed slightly.

Leave Westbank later than Kettle Vale departure because White Span only half mile away.

Arrive while still dark.

Measure wind/chop before first light.

Use same witness positions as morning where possible.

Fenner would place one cleaned metal basin on west-bank rise, filled from river before sunrise, left undisturbed beside sight frame.

Not to prove mechanism.

Just compare isolated surface with river surface during same sky.

No one would shade it, touch it, move it, or add objects during event.

Good.

Current slate plate could be offered as **supplemental local-approved observation only**, not core test.

I asked, "Worth it?"

Maro said, "If Fenner wants."

Vessa said, "Ask him."

Dask said, "Yes."

Nobody had asked Dask.

Sori wrote that down emotionally.

Not literally.

Probably.

Then Vessa looked at me.

"Shoulder?"

"Better."

"Hand?"

"Better."

"Sleep."

"Yes."

No argument.

There.

Definitely growth.

Upstairs, my room faced river.

Maro already asleep in other bed by time I finished checking bag.

Quietener wrapped.

Tavi's rock.

New slate current reader.

Renewal tin.

Knife.

Clothes.

Small pieces of a life temporarily carried instead of stored.

I put bag under bed.

Crutches against wall.

The reinforced bite marks caught moonlight from window.

Ugly.

Good.

Evidence.

Outside, Lume moved in dark.

Tomorrow it might reflect wrong sun again.

Might not.

Wind might break it.

Might reveal it differently.

Metal basin might show nothing.

Might show something.

Plate might be useful.

Might just become another object in bag.

I liked that.

Not uncertainty exactly.

Options.

I had thirteen copper.

A debt.

A repaired crutch.

A strange brass quietener I did not fully understand.

A one-copper river plate old ferries no longer wanted.

A home far south.

A river outside.

And tomorrow morning still unspent.

Not bad.
# CHAPTER 403

## THE OBSERVER

White Span looked different in wind.

Good.

If it had looked exactly the same, I would have been annoyed on principle.

We left Westbank while the inn sign still had both fake suns painted black against night.

Half mile.

Easy.

Cold enough to make shoulder complain before movement warmed it.

Not injured.

Just reminding me it existed.

Lessa waited at west rise with two lanterns, one broom, one dented wash basin, and no coffee.

"Fenner forgot coffee."

"Again?"

"He remembered basin."

"Tradeoffs."

She pointed toward bridge.

"Wind's here."

It was.

North to northeast.

Not strong.

Enough.

Lume's surface carried small diagonal ridges where yesterday had been broad calm sheet.

No mirror.

Not yet.

Dask was already happy.

I could tell because he had become quieter.

Dangerous sign.

Fenner came up hill carrying timing board under one arm and coffee under other.

Lessa looked betrayed.

"You remembered?"

"I contain multitudes."

"You contain one cup."

"Mine."

She took it.

"Now none."

Local command structure.

Efficient.

Vessa checked positions.

Same as yesterday where possible.

I took witness post.

Dask sight/timing.

Maro bank/weather.

Sori master record.

Kel bridge traffic and practical effects.

Fenner local sequence.

Lessa utility and insulting everyone.

Good team.

The basin sat on a waist-high stone table beside sight frame.

Clean enough.

Metal dull, not polished.

Filled from Lume before first light.

Water inside trembled slightly when gusts hit rim.

Not ideal isolated still surface.

Still useful.

Dask wanted to shield it.

Fenner said no.

"Same sky. Same wind. Different container. Don't improve test until after we see test."

Dask looked at me.

"He's right."

"I know."

"You looked upset."

"I am capable of being right and upset simultaneously."

There.

I liked him again.

My slate plate stayed wrapped in bag.

For now.

Fenner had approved supplemental use later if needed, but not before first observation pass.

Good.

No new toy contaminating baseline.

The east brightened.

Real sunrise came like yesterday.

Slow.

Normal.

Respectable.

Physical sun broke ridge.

Gold touched upper bridge.

We watched downstream of arch four.

Nothing.

One breath.

Ten.

Thirty.

Wind moved chop diagonally across river.

No false band.

Dask marked.

Fenner said nothing.

Lessa whispered, "Don't sulk at water."

"I'm not."

"You are."

Minute one.

Nothing broad.

Then Maro said, "There."

Not center.

Closer to west bank.

A narrow patch behind one projecting stone shoulder where surface chop weakened.

Pale gold.

Wrong direction.

Small.

Maybe six feet across.

It appeared in protected water while exposed water beside it stayed ordinary gray-gold from real east sun.

There.

New.

Not answer.

Dask's pencil moved.

My brain moved too.

Calm patch.

Shelter.

False reflection present locally.

Exposed chop no broad band.

Do not say requires calm.

Not yet.

The patch widened along sheltered edge maybe another three feet.

Stopped.

Wind gust hit.

Surface broke.

False light fragmented.

Not vanished.

Split into little flashes between ripples.

Then rejoined when water flattened for two breaths.

Good.

Very good.

Not because solved.

Because behavior.

I wrote:

**FALSE REFLECTION PRESENT IN PARTIALLY SHELTERED WEST-BANK WATER WHILE EXPOSED ADJACENT WATER REMAINED CHOPPED AND DID NOT FORM PRIOR BROAD BAND.**

Then:

**WITHIN SHELTERED PATCH, STRONGER RIPPLE FRAGMENTED VISIBLE BAND INTO DISCONTINUOUS FLASHES. LESS RIPPLE RESTORED MORE CONTINUOUS APPEARANCE.**

Sori read over once.

Nodded.

Dask said, "That suggests surface coherence threshold."

"Suggests," I said.

"Yes."

He actually used word correctly.

Progress was disgusting.

Basin.

I looked.

Nothing false.

It reflected east sky normally.

Metal rim vibrated slightly in wind.

Water inside had small ripples.

No west-facing gold.

Fenner saw too.

"Basin's boring."

"Useful boring," Sori said.

"Still boring."

Then Lessa said, "Wait."

We waited.

She crouched beside basin without touching.

One corner of basin sat behind sight-frame post.

Tiny sheltered wedge.

Water there was calmer than rest.

For maybe one second I thought pale gold flashed.

Maybe.

Then gone.

Dask inhaled.

I said, "No claim."

He exhaled.

Lessa said, "I saw something."

"So did I."

Sori: "What?"

"Possible pale flash in sheltered basin corner. Less than one breath. Could be real-sun glint, observer angle, rim reflection, or false phenomenon."

Dask said, "Record ambiguous."

"Yes."

There.

We did.

No miracle.

No clean lab answer.

Good.

False patch in river lasted longer than I expected.

Not six minutes broad.

Closer to four, depending whether you counted fragmented flashes as continuous event.

That became argument.

Dask wanted two timings.

Fenner wanted one operational time.

Sori solved it.

"Primary visible interval and continuous-band interval separately."

There.

Primary false-light presence: about four minutes fifty breaths by board.

Continuous sheltered band: about three minutes twenty breaths before stronger chop broke it mostly into intermittent fragments.

Then fragments continued perhaps another minute and change before nothing distinguishable remained.

No one liked approximate wording.

Reality remained rude.

Kel crossed bridge during event again.

No footing issue.

No visibility loss.

He reported false patch harder to notice from bridge deck today because wind broke surface.

Practical consequence.

Fenner reopened ferries sooner than yesterday because broad distracting band never formed.

That mattered.

Administrative hold shortened.

Not because danger lower proven.

Because distraction lower observed.

Toma Grell took first ferry.

Berrit complained he should have.

Toma told him spiritual carp could wait.

Good.

After false light vanished, Fenner approved my slate plate.

Not for anomaly.

Current.

We went down west bank to safe shelf.

Riva's plate set flat at waterline.

Maro helped choose position.

Wet.

Film pulled along grooves southeast with slight cross-bias eastward under north wind.

Matched local float board generally.

Good.

Useful object remained useful object.

No glowing.

No secret reaction.

Dask looked almost disappointed.

I was pleased.

"Current reader reads current," I said.

"Revolutionary."

"Write paper."

Sori said, "Don't."

We packed.

Then route changed.

Fenner had message from Ira Fen by noon rider.

Outside witness obligation complete after two mornings.

Continue extension **east along Lume** to **Bellweather Crossing** if crew willing and Vessa approves.

Reason was not another miracle waiting on schedule.

It was infrastructure.

Bellweather maintained a line of old river mirrors and ferry sight posts used for dawn navigation before modern markers.

Regional office wanted comparison because White Span phenomenon might depend on local geometry, local river bend, or broader river reach.

Not proof.

Comparison.

Bellweather was roughly nine road miles east.

One overnight stop possible at **Low Fen Orchard** halfway.

There.

World opened again.

Vessa read message twice.

"Optional extension through Bellweather, return routing after unless new operational reason."

Sori checked stamp.

"Valid."

Kel said, "Road?"

Fenner said, "East bank road dry. One old ferry stair washed out, detour marked."

Maro looked interested.

"Bellweather mirrors still there?"

Fenner shrugged.

"Some. Half used for hanging laundry last I saw."

Dask looked offended on behalf of mirrors.

Excellent.

Vessa looked around crew.

"We can stop here. Obligation met. Or continue."

No pressure.

Good.

I looked east.

Lume bent broad and bright through grasslands.

Nine miles.

Another place.

Another comparison.

Another bed not mine.

Home remained south.

Still there.

I wanted it.

Also wanted east.

Apparently this was my problem now.

"Continue," I said.

Maro nodded.

Kel: "Fine."

Sori: "If paperwork stays clean."

Dask said, "Bellweather has historical mirror infrastructure."

Vessa: "That is not a vote."

"Continue."

"Better."

We left White Span after midday meal.

No ceremony.

Fenner shook Vessa's hand.

Lessa gave Dask his own pencil cord back because he had left one yesterday.

Berrit told me fish had definitely been confused this morning.

Toma told him fish had definitely been fish.

I recorded neither.

Westbank faded behind.

The Two Suns sign visible longer than village because yellow paint was offensively bright.

Then bend took it.

East road followed Lume but stayed thirty to a hundred yards inland depending bank.

New grammar.

River always nearby.

Sometimes visible.

Sometimes hidden behind willow-like scrub and low white bluffs.

Sound came and went.

Flat boats moved downstream with square dark sails.

Road traffic more commercial than north basin.

Barrels.

Fruit carts.

Net bundles.

One wagon carrying six enormous ceramic jars tied individually in straw.

Dask wanted to know contents.

Driver shouted, "VINEGAR!"

Dask asked, "Why six jars?"

Driver shouted, "BECAUSE SEVEN BROKE THE AXLE!"

Good answer.

Shoulder did well first two miles.

Then began low ache.

I shifted bag.

Kel noticed.

Didn't ask.

At next shade stone he stopped mule for water.

Coincidence.

Probably not.

I took ten breaths.

Nobody counted aloud.

Crew had learned me.

That was strange.

Nice.

The road climbed away from Lume near afternoon.

Below, river surface flashed real sun correctly.

East afternoon light.

No second reflection.

Normal river could still be pretty after becoming evidence.

Important.

Around fourth mile we found first old river mirror.

Not at Bellweather.

A roadside remnant.

Tall stone post with rusted iron frame holding oval silvered plate tilted toward river.

Clouded almost black.

One corner cracked.

Laundry not present.

Dask stopped.

Vessa said, "Thirty seconds."

He approached without touching.

Stamp at base:

**BW-R3 / SIGHT 12**

Bellweather Reach 3 maybe.

Maro said, "Old dawn sight marker. Boatmen lined reflection with notch to read approach in fog."

"Magic?" I asked.

"Mirror."

Dask said, "Silver treatment sometimes directional."

Maro: "Mirror."

I liked Maro.

The plate reflected us badly.

Six stretched people.

One mule.

My head looked long.

Unacceptable.

No false sun.

No anomaly.

We moved.

Low Fen Orchard appeared near dusk.

Not much settlement.

An orchard on slightly raised island of dry ground, rows of low black-barked trees with pale green fruit, one long farmhouse, two worker sheds, road shelter, hitch rail.

Sign:

**LOW FEN ORCHARD / ROAD BEDS / PEAR BRANDY / NO CREDIT**

Promising.

Owner **Hedda Morn** met us with pruning knife still in hand.

Broad woman, gray braid, left knee stiff.

"Survey?"

Vessa showed stamp.

"Beds six?"

"Four beds. Two hammocks."

Sori opened mouth.

Hedda said, "Hammocks count if you sleep."

Sori closed mouth.

Interesting.

Vessa said, "Assignment coverage?"

"Road rate, yes. Dinner extra if not listed."

It was listed.

Good.

We had stew with pears in it.

I expected terrible.

It wasn't.

Dask hated it.

This made meal better.

After dinner Hedda poured tiny finger of pear brandy for herself, none for us unless paid.

I did not buy alcohol.

Mostly because shoulder and dawn schedule.

Also because one copper for bath had been smarter.

Maybe later.

Outside orchard, Lume glimmered through trees half mile away.

Tomorrow Bellweather.

Old mirrors.

Different river geometry.

Comparison rather than answer.

That felt right.

I checked bag before hammock.

Quietener.

Slate reader.

Tavi rock.

Renewal paste.

Thirteen copper.

No magic attempts.

No fights.

No solution.

But we knew more.

Wind chop mattered to visible form.

Shelter mattered enough to produce local patch.

Isolated basin did not clearly reproduce effect, though one ambiguous flash existed.

Current stayed current.

Ferries changed procedure based on observed distraction.

And route moved east.

Observer.

Not solver.

For now, better.
# CHAPTER 404

## THE COMPARER

Hedda Morn woke us with a spoon against a pot.

Not bell.

Spoon.

Three hard strikes from farmhouse kitchen.

Dask sat upright in hammock and hit head on beam.

"Fuck."

Hedda shouted through wall.

"Breakfast!"

Sori opened one eye.

"Efficient system."

I had slept in bed.

Rank had privileges.

Or disability.

Same result sometimes.

My shoulder was stiff when I first moved it.

Not sharp.

Not new.

I rolled it slowly.

Forward.

Side.

Better than Greyhook.

Hand closed around crutch grip without complaint until last bit of squeeze.

Also better.

Right crutch wrap still dark where Rusk's resin had filled tooth marks.

Still ugly.

Still mine.

I stood.

No drama.

Breakfast was oats with pear.

Of course.

Pear bread.

Pear preserve.

And something Hedda called orchard tea that tasted like hot bark remembering fruit.

Kel drank twice.

"Good."

Hedda looked at him.

"No."

He drank third time anyway.

Maro asked road condition.

"Dry," Hedda said. "East ditch soft after marker six. Don't step in it."

Dask said, "Why marker six specifically?"

"Because that's where ditch is soft."

"I mean what caused it?"

"Water."

"From where?"

Hedda pointed spoon toward ceiling.

"Sky."

Dask looked at me.

I ate pear.

No help.

We left first bell.

Low Fen Orchard disappeared behind black-barked trees in twenty minutes.

Bellweather road stayed close to Lume now.

Closer than yesterday.

Sometimes river only thirty yards away beyond willow scrub.

Sometimes road climbed white shelf and water dropped below us, broad and brown-green with silver where morning touched it.

No wrong sun.

Physical sun east.

Reflection where geometry expected.

Good.

Or boring.

Boring was data.

Dask looked at river every opening.

Sori finally said, "If you turn your head any farther, it comes off."

"I am observing."

"You're walking into Maro."

He corrected course.

Maro said, "Observed."

I liked route crew.

At second mile, old sight posts became frequent.

Not every hundred yards.

Maybe every half mile where road and river aligned.

Stone uprights.

Iron frames.

Some empty.

Some held blackened oval plates.

One had been repurposed to hang laundry.

Dask stopped.

Vessa did not.

He caught up.

Growth.

Maro explained while walking.

"Bellweather used mirrors before bank lamps got cheap. Fog sits low. Boatmen couldn't always see far shore. Sight plates caught dawn or lamp and gave line."

"Mirror."

"Treatment could have directional response."

"Mirror."

"Those statements aren't mutually exclusive."

"Still mirror."

Sori said, "I'm putting that on your grave."

Maro considered.

"Fine."

At marker six, ditch was soft.

We didn't step in it.

Revolutionary.

Bellweather announced itself by sound.

Hammers.

Bells.

Boat horns.

People yelling numbers.

Then smell.

Tar.

Coal smoke.

Wet wood.

Fish.

Something sweet frying.

Then town.

Bellweather Crossing was bigger than Westbank and Kettle Vale combined.

Not Carrow-big.

Different.

Long instead of dense.

Town stretched along both banks with bridge at center and ferry docks above and below.

Main bridge was iron-and-stone, three broad arches, newer than White Span.

Upstream stood older crossing remains.

Two massive stone piers with no deck between them.

Each pier carried a tall frame of silvered plates arranged like vertical fan.

There.

River mirrors.

Not one.

Dozens.

Most blackened.

Some bright.

One missing.

Dask made noise.

Not word.

Noise.

Sori said, "Control yourself."

"I am."

"Worse."

A road clerk met us at west checkpoint.

Woman named **Pera Lonn**.

Short.

Round glasses.

Blue ink stripe down left sleeve.

She read Ira's extension paper twice.

"White Span wrong dawn."

Vessa said, "Observed six mornings total, two outside-witness mornings."

"And you brought Renn."

Dask brightened.

Pera pointed at me.

"Him."

I sighed.

"Why?"

"Dog story."

"Zero dead."

"Heard fifteen."

"Inflation."

Pera looked at crutches.

"You fought fifteen dogs on those?"

"I did not fight fifteen dogs."

"How many?"

"Enough."

Pera nodded.

Work replaced gossip.

Pera held up finger.

He exhaled.

"Understood."

Good.

No repeated dawn.

Comparison by records and infrastructure.

Bellweather archive occupied second floor above ferry office.

Stairs.

Of course.

Twenty-eight.

I counted because body did.

Sori noticed because she notices everything annoying.

"Need stop?"

"No."

At top shoulder warm.

Fine.

Archive smelled like dust, river damp, and old leather.

Pera handed us to **Olden Marr**, archivist.

He wore fingerless gloves despite warmth.

First thing he said:

"I haven't."

Olden pulled four ledgers.

Olden looked over glasses.

"If there were, I assume that's why you're here."

"Yes."

Simple.

Dask passed exam.

We split ledgers.

Not read every page.

Thank gods.

Olden had indexes.

Season.

Visibility.

Mirror faults.

Fog.

Glare.

False lamp.

Sun alignment.

Boat incidents.

We searched terms around reflection anomalies.

There were many normal problems.

Morning glare blinding eastbound pilot.

Fog doubling lamps.

Ice on plates creating split highlights.

Bird shit.

More bird shit.

A note from twenty-three years ago:

**SOUTH ARRAY SHOWED TWO DAWNS. CLEANED GULL RESIDUE. RESOLVED.**

Dask stared.

"Technically two dawns."

Olden said, "Technically gull shit."

Sori laughed loud enough to get shushed by another clerk.

Useful absence accumulated.

Forty-two years indexed.

No persistent west-facing sunrise on river.

No multi-minute wrong-direction surface reflection matching White Span description.

No record of bridge shadow failing to extinguish a false river reflection.

No recurring calm-water-only west band.

That did not prove Bellweather couldn't do it tomorrow.

But it mattered.

White Span looked more local.

Or newer.

Or unnoticed elsewhere.

Or dependent on geometry Bellweather lacked.

Many options.

Good.

Olden brought a map.

Lume bent differently here.

At White Span river ran east-southeast.

Bellweather crossing sat on long north-south bend before river turned east again.

Old mirror arrays faced southeast and southwest from old piers.

"Why two directions?" I asked.

Olden tapped map.

"Morning fog. One array caught dawn. Other caught bank lamps. Later both caught lamps depending season."

"So not symmetrical use."

"No."

Dask said, "Were plates differently treated?"

"Yes."

Maro looked betrayed.

Olden continued.

"Morning plates had blue-black backing. Lamp plates red-brown. Silver wash same family. Different backing reduced glare."

Dask looked at Maro.

Maro said, "Mirror."

Fine.

We went to lunch.

Ferry office fed assignment crew lentil soup and fried river cakes.

I bought nothing.

Thirteen copper survived noon.

Pera joined us halfway through.

"Keeper available. North pier only. South access closed because someone dropped wrench through ladder yesterday and decided gravity was management's problem."

Kel said, "Was it?"

"Eventually."

North pier access was ground-level walkway from bank to old stone base.

No climbing.

Good.

Keeper **Jori Pell** met us there.

Maro looked at him.

Jori looked at Maro.

"No."

Maro blinked.

"I didn't ask."

"Everyone asks."

Dask said, "Are you related?"

Both men said, "No."

Excellent.

Jori was younger, maybe twenty-seven, thick black hair and one gold tooth.

He carried maintenance satchel full of cloths, oil, gauges, and a little square viewing hood.

Six serviceable north plates remained on old fan array.

Each oval roughly forearm long.

Silver face slightly smoked.

Back dark blue-black.

Frames could rotate limited arc and tilt.

Stops prevented full turn.

Not mystical.

Engineering.

Old engineering was still engineering.

Jori demonstrated without changing stored calibration.

He opened one viewing hood around lower plate.

"Cuts side glare. Look from mark."

Brass foot mark embedded in stone.

I looked.

Plate reflected bright patch of southern sky and thin line of river.

Move head two inches.

Reflection changed sharply.

Directional by geometry and hood.

Not magic necessarily.

Dask looked after permission.

Sori after him.

Maro.

Kel.

Vessa.

Then Jori said, "White Span people describe light staying under bridge shadow?"

"Yes," Vessa said.

"Mirrors can't tell you about that."

Dask said, "Not directly."

"Not indirectly either unless you invent story."

I liked him too.

Jori showed backing.

Blue-black layer had fine mineral flecks.

"Glare cut. Helps dawn edge show in fog."

"Magical treatment?" Dask asked.

Jori shrugged.

"Silver wash takes charge during making. Backing takes some. Once made, plate mostly plate. You want guild answer, ask mirror guild. You want ferry answer, it reflects things."

Maro smiled.

Vindicated.

I asked, "Any plate ever show source not actually in front of it?"

Jori scratched chin.

"Cracked ones can double. Bent ones shift. Backing peel makes ghosts. Fog makes idiots."

"Persistent wrong direction?"

"Not if plate healthy."

"River surface?"

"River does what river wants."

Not answer.

Accurate.

Dask asked to inspect maintenance records.

Jori pointed back toward archive.

"Olden has them."

Dask visibly suffered.

We had just left archive.

Vessa said, "Later if needed."

There.

Restraint.

Then something useful happened.

Not anomaly.

Money.

Pera found us at pier.

"Regional office sent pay clarification. Extension days count as field days."

Sori immediately said, "Starting day four."

Pera nodded.

"Yes. Your original route language. Two copper per completed field day after third. Merecross already paid departure six. North extension didn't void terms."

I stopped looking at mirror.

There.

Economy.

"How many completed paid days do you have logged?" Sori asked.

Pera checked slip.

"Three additional since threshold, through yesterday. Today pays on completion."

I did arithmetic.

Six copper accrued.

Not paid yet.

Today would make eight accrued after workday complete.

Sori looked at me.

"Don't spend it before paid."

"I wasn't."

"You stopped looking at the mirror when she said eight copper."

Fuck everyone knowing my face.

Pera said, "Bellweather can settle regional extension pay tomorrow morning if Vessa signs tonight's completion. Or carry ledger onward."

Vessa said, "Settle here."

Good.

Tomorrow potentially eight copper.

Thirteen to twenty-one.

Vale still twenty-three.

Interesting.

Not rich.

But closer to something.

Artifact markets got different when purse crossed twenty.

I did not say that.

Sori would hear anyway.

She narrowed eyes.

I looked innocent.

Poorly.

We spent late afternoon comparing Bellweather's present river surface to White Span notes.

Not formal anomaly watch.

Just ordinary observation.

Wind light southwest.

Water moderate ripple.

Real sun west now because afternoon.

Reflections normal.

WS-F/9 plate stayed in bag.

No reason.

Quietener stayed in bag.

Even less reason.

Good tools did not demand use.

That was maybe most important thing about owning them.

At fifth bell, Vessa closed workday.

Pera signed local completion.

Sori copied pay note.

Dask asked one final question about backing mineral composition.

Olden sent him to mirror guild three streets uphill.

He looked at Vessa.

"Tomorrow," she said.

"Before departure?"

"Maybe."

He accepted maybe like man swallowing bone.

Bellweather lodging was above old ferry tavern.

Six beds.

No hammocks.

Luxury.

Dinner not included.

Assignment rate covered room, not food.

There.

Economy again.

Tavern board:

**STEW + BREAD - 2 BITS**

**FRIED RIVER CAKES - 3 BITS**

**MEAT PIE - 5 BITS**

Bits.

Still no universal conversion.

I had bits.

Unspecified amount.

Annoying even internally.

I bought stew and bread.

Paid in bits.

Copper remained thirteen.

No need to invent conversion because cashier knew and I didn't care enough.

Freedom.

Sori sat across from me.

"You're pleased."

"Food."

"Pay."

"Also pay."

"Eight tomorrow if signed."

"Apparently."

"Twenty-one."

"Stop."

"Vale twenty-three."

"I know."

"Almost symmetry."

"Debt is not collectible set."

"You collect worse things."

She had point.

Kel joined with meat pie.

"What's next after Bellweather?"

Vessa sat down at end table with Pera's route note.

"Regional office gave two options."

Of course.

She unfolded paper.

"One: turn south along old ferry road toward Merecross network. Not Carrow directly. Two: continue east to **Sable Quay**, where Lume widens into trade basin."

Dask appeared from nowhere.

"Sable Quay has mirror guild."

Vessa stared.

"How do you know?"

"Olden."

"Of course."

Maro sat.

"How far?"

"Eleven miles. Road good. One night likely at **Rill House** or camp depending pace."

Sori asked, "Operational reason?"

Vessa read.

"Bellweather comparison suggests White Span behavior not historically common here. Regional office wants records delivered to Sable Quay survey annex because Quay handles lower-Lume traffic and has broader sight-system archive. Extension authorized if crew willing."

There.

Again.

A legitimate door.

Not quest.

Paperwork.

Best kind.

Kel said, "East."

Maro nodded.

Dask was already spiritually in mirror guild.

Sori looked at me.

"Don't say market."

I hadn't.

Now I was thinking it.

Sable Quay.

Trade basin.

Eleven miles farther from home.

Twenty-one copper tomorrow if pay settled.

Dangerous combination.

Vessa said, "Greg?"

I ate last bread.

Shoulder low ache.

Hand almost normal.

Crutch sound.

Bag slightly heavier than when I left Carrow.

Map much heavier.

"East," I said.

Sori sighed.

"He means market."

"I mean east."

"Same face."

Fuck my face.

Outside, old Bellweather mirrors caught evening lamps one by one.

Not wrong light.

Just light.

That mattered.

White Span had shown us something strange.

Bellweather showed us what forty-two years of ordinary strange looked like when people bothered to write it down.

Glare.

Fog.

Cracks.

Ice.

Bird shit.

Normal failures.

Normal explanations.

Comparison did not solve the wrong sunrise.

It did something better.

It made the mystery smaller without making it less interesting.

Local.

Maybe.

New.

Maybe.

Geometry-dependent.

Maybe.

At least not obviously everywhere.

That was enough.

Tomorrow I would collect eight copper.

Then we would go east.

Apparently that was what my life did now.

Compare one place to another until map became too large to pretend I was only visiting.
# CHAPTER 405

## THE EARNER

Bellweather paid me in the morning.

That was satisfying.

Not poetic.

Better.

Pera Lonn had three papers, two stamps, one clerk beside her, and the expression of a woman who believed money should only move after paperwork had suffered enough.

"Vessa Harn signed completion. Local extension verified. Four payable field days. Two copper each. Eight copper."

She pushed a small cloth pouch across desk.

I picked it up.

Weight.

Real.

Not theoretical money.

Sori said, "Count it."

"I trust bureaucracy."

Pera looked offended.

"Don't."

Fair.

I counted.

Eight.

Thirteen became twenty-one.

Vale remained twenty-three.

Not close enough to matter.

Sori watched me put the pouch away.

"Don't."

"Again, haven't said anything."

"Purchases."

"Same posture."

"Depends carts. Foot crews pass faster."

"Mules?"

"Controlled batches."

"I regret mentioning mirror guild."

Pera pointed at him.

"Then I regret you."

He kept walking.

We left before second bell.

Twenty-one copper felt different in purse.

Not because weight.

Because choices.

At thirteen, some prices ended conversation.

At twenty-one, they became questions.

Still not yes.

Question.

Could afford did not mean should buy.

This was adulthood.

Terrible system.

East road out of Bellweather widened quickly.

Commercial road.

Two carts abreast in places.

Packed gravel instead of hard dirt.

Stone drainage.

Mile markers maintained enough to deserve numbers.

East of Bellweather it started behaving like infrastructure.

Docks every mile or two.

Short loading ramps.

Tether posts.

Warehouses standing alone beside road for no obvious town.

Flatboats moved downstream under dark square sails, heavy enough that water climbed their sides.

One carried stacked blue ceramic jars.

Another carried timber.

Another something under canvas that smelled like pepper even from road.

Things moved because someone wanted them somewhere else badly enough to pay.

Simple motivation.

Complicated world.

Around mile three we passed a roadside exchange board.

Not market.

Prices.

Freight listings nailed under awning.

**BELLWEATHER -> SABLE QUAY**

**BARREL SPACE**

**HALF CRATE**

**LIVE BIRDS EXTRA**

**NO OPEN OIL**

Vessa said, "Considering cart?"

He nodded.

"Shoulder?" she asked me.

"Fine."

Not perfectly.

Fine.

Low ache only after first hour.

Hand mostly normal.

Current body was coming back online.

Kel said, "Walking keeps us flexible. Cart batch could save two hours if timing good."

Sori said, "Costs?"

"Assignment transport only if route need documented."

Vessa looked at road.

"No need yet."

Good.

We walked.

At mile five, trade road split around a low quarry cut.

Main carts took lower stone lane.

Sable Quay first appeared from there.

Not town.

Shape.

Buildings clustered on both banks and on low artificial-looking islands or piers reaching into water.

Masts.

Cranes.

Smoke.

Three bridges visible from miles away.

One high and narrow.

One broad.

One maybe rail or freight-only.

Dask stopped walking.

Sori said, "Walk."

"I am."

"Not currently."

Maro shaded eyes.

"Bigger than last time."

"Nine years."

"How much bigger?"

"That east crane field wasn't there."

There.

World changing without us.

Good.

Sable Quay became destination instead of concept.

And then road made us pay for looking.

Mile nine freight-control rotation.

Pera had not lied.

East embankment work narrowed road to one reinforced lane between river drop and active stonework.

A red-cloth control post held maybe thirty carts.

Foot traffic could pass in side corridor.

Mules could not.

Our shared cases rode two pack mules.

There.

Delay.

Not crisis.

A control woman named **Tess Arlo** explained.

"Mule batch in thirty-five minutes if no westbound priority. Forty-five if stone train comes. Foot crew can go now, animals stay here with registered handler."

Vessa looked at Kel.

Kel looked at cases.

"I stay."

Sori said, "Custody?"

"I'll sign hold."

Vessa considered.

"We split?"

Normally I disliked split parties.

Nobody acknowledged him.

Vessa decided.

Sori shook head.

Vessa assigned.

Kel with mules/cases.

Reasonable.

Guard rope on one side.

Stonework on other.

Workers set dressed blocks into embankment using tripod hoists and shouted cadence.

Not magical spectacle.

Labor.

One foreman used a little brass level that flashed green when stone sat true.

I noticed.

Kept walking.

Important reminder.

I did.

Loose hauling line crossed path knee-high for two breaths.

They lifted.

No performance.

Normal accommodation between strangers doing work.

Good.

Two stone pylons framing road with hanging boards listing fees by wagon, beast, barrel, dock class, and probably phases of moon.

Excellent.

Sable Quay had systems colliding.

Dock bells.

Auction calls.

Cart wheels.

Boat horns.

Saw mills.

Metal striking metal.

People yelling berth numbers.

People yelling prices.

People yelling because everyone else was yelling.

Buildings leaned commercial.

Tall warehouses, narrow offices, inns stacked over shops, guild signs, weighing houses, rope halls, chandlers, repair yards.

The river basin occupied center of everything.

Water wide enough that opposite bank looked like another district instead of across street.

Cargo cranes swung over barges.

One barge carried an entire small house.

Dask said, "Mirror guild."

I said, "Survey annex."

He looked at me.

"Yes."

Pain.

We found annex first.

Good people.

Three-story stone building beside west basin office.

Sign:

**LOWER LUME SURVEY ANNEX**

Below:

**TRAFFIC / SIGHT / FLOW / INCIDENT RECORDS**

Inside smelled like ink and wet coats.

A clerk named **Nema Vos** took Vessa's packet and immediately became alarmingly competent.

She was maybe thirty, dark curls tied high, sleeves rolled, six pencils behind one ear.

Six.

Dask looked at pencils.

She noticed.

"Don't."

He looked impressed.

Vessa summarized White Span and Bellweather in five minutes.

Nema asked good questions.

"White Span six consecutive mornings?"

"Yes."

"Two outside-witness?"

"Yes."

"Broad band calm morning, sheltered patch choppy morning?"

"Yes."

"None in forty-two surviving indexed years."

"Cause?"

"Unknown."

"Not established."

Nema nodded.

"Good. Keep it that way until reason."

Dask and I both liked her.

Dangerous.

There.

Choice existed.

Not automatic.

Vessa asked, "Any reason yet?"

Nema looked toward ceiling like records lived above it.

"Maybe. Not the exciting kind."

Best kind.

She pulled one thin folder.

"Three ferry captains reported unusual dawn glare this week near **Glassmouth Reach**, two miles east of Quay basin. Not wrong-direction sunrise. Not multi-minute band. Just glare strong enough to obscure channel marks for seconds at a time. Could be ordinary angle because water level dropped four inches."

Dask inhaled.

Nema held up hand.

"Could be ordinary angle."

He closed mouth.

"We're checking tomorrow anyway. If you're still here, outside eyes useful. If not, your White Span packet stands alone."

Good.

No railroad.

Nema stamped receipt.

"Your cases?"

"Delayed at mile nine," Vessa said.

"Fine. Bring by third bell."

Sori handed seal numbers.

Nema checked.

"Lodging?"

"Not arranged."

"Survey rate at Dockhouse Seven if rooms open. If full, Rill House west road or private inns. Food not covered unless assigned overnight work."

Economy.

Excellent.

Then she said dangerous thing.

"Mirror guild is two streets north."

Dask smiled.

Sori looked at her.

"Why would you tell him?"

Nema looked at Dask.

"Because I want to see what happens."

Chaos clerk.

We had maybe one bell before Kel arrived.

Vessa said, "One bell. No purchases for assignment. Personal time. Stay in west basin district."

There.

Freedom.

I did not immediately go to market.

Important.

I went with Dask to mirror guild.

Different.

Guild occupied narrow brick building with black glass windows.

Sign showed silver oval crossed by blue line.

Inside, front room displayed mirrors.

Not household mirrors.

Signal plates.

Sight plates.

Inspection mirrors.

Heat-reading dark glass.

Tiny convex mirrors for machine housings.

Long narrow pieces mounted in brass.

Prices.

Oh.

There were prices.

**FOG SIGHT PLATE, NEW - 18C**

**LAMPSIDE GHOST CHECKER - 11C**

**SILVER-BACK FIELD MIRROR - 9C**

**SPLIT-ANGLE CALIBRATION PAIR - 27C**

**RIVER DAWN PLATE, BLUE-BACK - 34C**

There.

Twenty-one copper suddenly became medium money.

Useful.

Not enough.

Exactly right.

A guild woman approached.

**Elya Senn**, badge said.

Forties.

Shaved head.

Silver dust embedded in cuffs.

"Survey?"

Dask said, "Yes."

I said, "Personal browsing."

She looked at my crutches, then bag, then Dask's face.

"Which one is dangerous?"

"Him," I said.

Dask said, "Probably him."

Fair.

Elya asked what we wanted.

Dask launched into Bellweather plate backing.

I wandered.

Not far.

Still listened.

Elya explained blue-black dawn backing reduced off-axis glare and improved contrast, yes, but no, plates did not create light.

Normal.

Then I found used shelf.

Danger.

Not junk.

Guild-inspected used.

Tags had condition grades and reason retired.

Better danger.

A palm-sized folding inspection mirror with edge chipped.

4c.

A two-piece sight bracket missing one clamp.

3c.

A narrow smoked plate retired for backing peel.

6c.

A little brass housing containing three rotating glass slits.

Tag:

**PARALLAX FINDER, PF-3**

**USED / GRADE C**

**10C**

**FAULT: CENTER DETENT SLIPS UNDER VIBRATION**

I picked it up only after checking sign said handling allowed.

Heavy for size.

Three slits aligned different angles when ring turned.

Old field tool for checking whether apparent offset came from observer position or target displacement.

Interesting.

Very interesting.

Ten copper.

I had twenty-one.

Vale twenty-three.

Half my liquid almost.

No.

Not immediate.

Good.

Elya appeared beside me.

"That one bites people who love clever tools."

"Because detent slips?"

"Because ten copper feels cheap compared to thirty-six new."

"How much repair?"

"If only spring, two to four. If ring channel worn, six to nine. If axle bent, throw it at enemy."

Rational price.

"Use?"

"Line-of-sight comparison. Surveyors. Machine aligners. Mirror fitters. People who think their eyes are trustworthy until tool insults them."

I wanted it.

Problem.

Could it change options?

Yes.

Would I use it beyond current river mystery?

Probably.

Could I afford ten?

Yes.

Should I spend nearly half current liquid on another bounded problem while owing Vale twenty-three?

Different question.

I put it back.

Elya nodded.

"Good."

"What?"

"Worse."

"Agreed."

Dask arrived.

Saw PF-3.

Made noise.

I said, "No."

"I didn't say anything."

"Your face."

There.

Justice.

We left without buying.

Twenty-one survived mirror guild.

This deserved medal.

Outside, Sable Quay market district spilled north.

I could see rows of awnings.

Hear auction bell.

Smell spice, hot metal, fried dough.

I did not go.

Not yet.

One bell meant one bell.

Crew before market.

Painful maturity.

Kel arrived at annex near third bell with mules and cases.

Delay had been forty-two minutes.

He looked annoyed.

"Stone train."

"Food?" he asked.

Maro handed him fried bread he'd bought in street.

Kel immediately forgave civilization.

Cases checked in.

Seal intact.

Nema countersigned delivery.

Vessa closed route segment.

Then asked crew what we wanted.

Not work assignment yet.

Today could end here.

Tomorrow optional Glassmouth observation if we remained.

Sori said, "We should stay one night at least. Cases just arrived."

Kel said, "Agreed."

Maro said, "Glassmouth is two miles. Might as well look if annex wants outside eyes."

Dask said, "Mirror guild opens first bell."

Everyone ignored him.

Vessa looked at me.

Sable Quay outside.

Twenty-one copper.

A ten-copper parallax finder sitting on used shelf.

Market I hadn't entered.

Home much farther west than I'd planned weeks ago.

Shoulder almost normal.

Purse healthier because I had worked.

This mattered.

Not luck.

Not found money.

Not inheritance.

Labor.

Field days.

I had been useful long enough that road paid me for remaining useful.

I liked that more than expected.

Vessa nodded.

"One night. Glassmouth dawn if annex confirms. Then reassess."

Good.

We got Dockhouse Seven rooms.

Survey rate.

Two rooms, three beds each.

Food personal.

I bought a hot meat bun from street for one bit.

Bits remained unspecified.

Copper stayed twenty-one.

Then, finally, I walked market.

Not to buy.

To look.

Mostly.

Sori came with me because she did not trust "mostly."

Sable Quay market was not twelve tables.

It was streets.

Tool row.

River row.

Salvage row.

Textile court.

Spice lane.

Auction yard.

Used magical hardware behind wire screens with licensed sellers.

Prices that made twenty-one copper look like childhood allowance.

Forty.

Sixty.

One hundred twenty.

Silver marks.

Gold once, on a locked case I did not even approach.

There.

Economic ceiling moved upward.

Not because world got more expensive.

Because I had reached market where expensive things lived.

Important distinction.

Sori watched me realize.

"Happy?"

"Extremely."

"Also true."

"Growth."

"Temporary."

She laughed.

Inside sat a squat iron ring the size of dinner plate with six engraved notches and a tag:

**LOAD-SHARE COLLAR / RETIRED DOCK CRANE / 48C**

Known use notes listed.

Known failure notes listed.

Price forty-eight.

Could not afford it.

Not remotely with Vale.

And that was fine.

Better than fine.

Good.

Money had direction now.

Not hoard.

Access.

Option.

Future yes.

We walked back at dusk.

Sable basin lights came on one dock at a time.

Mirrored in water normally.

Hundreds of them.

No wrong sun.

Just commerce.

Twenty-three owed.

A bag of small tools.

A body mostly recovered.

A crew that had somehow become people I expected beside me at dinner.

Excellent.

Tomorrow, maybe Glassmouth.

# CHAPTER 406

## THE CONTRACTOR

Sable Quay woke before I did.

That was offensive.

By first gray light, carts were already rattling over stone below Dockhouse Seven.

Somewhere close, someone hammered metal in steady groups of four.

A crane bell rang twice.

Then once.

Then three times.

Probably meaningful.

To someone.

I lay still another ten breaths.

Luxury.

Shoulder felt mostly normal until I lifted arm high.

Then low reminder.

Hand closed clean around crutch grip.

Good.

Body debt shrinking.

Money debt not.

Twenty-one copper.

Twenty-three Vale.

Near symmetry remained annoying.

I got dressed.

Maro was already awake, sitting at window with tea.

"Glassmouth?" I asked.

"Messenger came."

"And?"

"Annex says no need."

Excellent.

"Ordinary?"

"Probably."

"Probably isn't observed."

"You've been around Dask too long."

"Terrible illness."

Good.

Boring solved itself.

Even better.

At bottom:

**IF YOUR CREW IS AVAILABLE, COME ANNEX AFTER BREAKFAST. POSSIBLE SHORT CONTRACT. NOT MIRRORS.**

There.

Dangerous words.

Not mirrors.

I liked them immediately.

Breakfast downstairs was two eggs, dark bread, and something advertised as river sausage.

I bought bread and eggs.

Bits.

Copper untouched.

Sori watched me pay.

"No."

"You looked."

"At money."

"That's ledger with anxiety."

"I have no anxiety."

"Twenty-one."

"Stop."

Kel arrived carrying coffee and no visible pear products.

He looked spiritually repaired.

Dask appeared last.

He had silver dust on one cuff.

Vessa saw it.

"You went guild before breakfast."

"No."

Sori looked at cuff.

Dask looked at cuff.

"Briefly."

"Did you buy anything?" Vessa asked.

"No."

I said, "Good."

Dask looked at me.

"You have no authority."

"Correct. Still good."

We reached Lower Lume Survey Annex after first bell.

Quay looked different in morning.

Not prettier.

More honest.

Yesterday, scale had been visual.

Cranes.

Bridges.

Warehouse roofs.

Markets.

Carts entering tax arch in two lanes.

Cargo slings moving every minute.

Flatboats waiting three deep at one dock.

Porters carrying numbered boards.

Clerks shouting weights.

Everything moving because someone expected something to arrive somewhere else.

Sable Quay had systems for work becoming volume.

Nema Vos stood behind annex counter with seven pencils today.

"One migrated," Dask said.

She pointed at him.

"Don't count them."

"I wasn't."

"You were."

Good.

Nema waved us into side room.

No archive.

Thank gods.

Table.

Map.

Three forms.

Better.

"Glassmouth closed local," she said. "Water dropped, eastern channel marker sat against direct glare angle, shading panel was two notches off because hinge pin wore. Fixed."

Dask said, "So captains were correct about unusual glare."

"Yes."

"And wrong about unusual cause."

"Mostly."

"Good."

Nema looked at him.

"You enjoyed that too much."

"No."

"That was an enthusiastic good."

Sori made sound like victory.

Nema tapped map.

"This is unrelated to your river-light work. Different ask."

Map showed south edge of Quay basin and a narrow industrial spur called **Blackglass Cut**.

"Dock Eight transfer yard has three retired load frames being moved to salvage auction tomorrow. One failed inspection last week. The other two were taken out with it because same production lot and nobody trusts cousins after one bites."

Kel said, "What failed?"

"One collar released late under lateral swing. No injury. Damaged crate. Yard shut frame."

There.

Load-share collars.

My brain remembered forty-eight copper one from market.

Nema continued.

"Dock wants independent pre-salvage function record so auction sheet distinguishes dead iron from restricted-use parts. Survey annex can provide two people. Dock wants four. Your crew has relevant field/load experience and records discipline."

Vessa asked, "Duration?"

"Half day. Maybe less if weather holds."

"Pay?"

Nema smiled.

There.

Contract.

"Separate from route pay. Dock Eight pays three copper per external hand for inspection witness and handling. Four if you accept controlled unloaded-motion test on designated frame."

Kel said, "Per person?"

"Per approved external hand. Not everyone needs to take it."

# CHAPTER 407

## THE BIDDER

Auctions were dangerous because they turned not buying something into losing.

That was bullshit.

Very effective bullshit.

I knew this before breakfast.

Knowing did not help.

Sori found me in Dockhouse Seven common room with the Dock Eight auction notice flattened beside my bowl.

"No."

"Good morning."

"You're studying it."

"Reading."

"Same thing when you want something."

"I don't know if I want anything."

She sat across from me.

"Worse."

The notice listed twelve lots.

Frames A, B, and C were not twelve separate lots because auctioneers understood temptation better than engineers.

**LOT 4: BK-12 TRANSFER FRAME A, RESTRICTED OPERATIONAL, COMPLETE**

**LOT 5: BK-17 TRANSFER FRAME B, REPAIR / PARTS**

**LOT 6: BK-17 TRANSFER FRAME C, SERVICEABLE UNLOADED, LOADED RECERTIFICATION REQUIRED**

Then smaller component lots.

Guide rollers.

Jaw assemblies.

Stop pins.

Spring housings.

Two old lateral collars from unrelated frames.

There.

Box.

Always box.

Sori followed eyes.

"No."

"You don't know what I'm looking at."

"Mixed hardware."

"How?"

"You like boxes where seller admits ignorance."

That was unfair.

Accurate.

Still unfair.

"Apparently."

"I'm going."

Sori looked at him.

"Why?"

"Frame C."

"You're buying a transfer frame?"

"No. Want to see what it sells for."

There.

Normal person.

I could learn.

Vessa entered behind him.

No field coat.

That changed her more than expected.

Still Vessa.

Just woman having breakfast instead of route authority.

"Annex has nothing for us," she said. "We're off assignment unless we accept something new."

Dask appeared from stairs.

"Mirror guild opens at second bell."

Sori pointed at him.

"Also no."

"I didn't ask you."

"Practicing."

Maro came last.

He looked rested.

Annoying.

"Duskport packet leaves fourth bell," he said.

I looked at him.

Sori closed eyes.

"Of course you asked."

Maro shrugged.

"Route board was there."

"Cost?" Kel asked.

"Three copper passenger deck. Five with bunk allotment if space. Freight separate."

There.

Duskport had price now.

Three copper.

Not much.

Which made it more dangerous.

"How long?" I asked.

"One day and one night if river behaves. Arrives next morning or midday."

"How far?"

"Packet clerk said about thirty river miles. Road longer."

Thirty.

Carrow got farther away without moving.

Sori watched me look at the route board.

"Duskport?"

"Maybe."

"Market?"

"Probably."

"Idiot."

"Sometimes."

Vessa poured tea.

"We decide after auction. No rush. Daily packet means daily."

Good.

No artificial deadline.

That made choice more real.

I hated it.

Dock Eight public viewing started before bell two.

Auction yard looked different with buyers.

Today everything had prices waiting to happen.

Dealers wore chalk boards on belts.

Repair shops sent apprentices with measuring sticks.

Two freight companies had men in clean coats pretending not to know each other.

A woman with three gold rings inspected frame feet by tapping them with knuckle.

Bran Tey stood near rail with arms folded.

Same jaw stripe.

Same folded ear.

He saw us.

"Morning."

Longest thing he'd ever said.

Kel nodded toward C.

"Viewing open?"

"Yes. Don't cycle."

"Wouldn't."

Bran looked at me.

"You bidding?"

"Maybe."

"Don't buy B."

I laughed.

He didn't.

"I wasn't planning to."

"Good."

That was probably illegal auction advice.

Or friendship.

Hard to tell with Bran.

Frame A drew serious attention.

Complete operational hardware had value even restricted.

Frame C too.

B attracted scavengers.

People cared less about whole failed frame than which pieces could be certified separately.

I cared about pieces too.

That was problem.

I walked lots once without touching.

Then again with Kel.

Lot 8 held two lateral collars.

Neither from B.

Different lots.

One had a stop tooth chipped.

Not useful enough.

Lot 9: jaw assemblies.

Heavy.

No.

Maybe useful if I owned transfer frame.

I did not.

Generic enough to be useful to someone.

Not me.

Mixed BK hardware.

Four worn guide shims.

Three spring seats.

There.

"That?"

"Maybe."

Old industrial term.

Diagnostic aid.

Not active control.

Not power source.

Not valuable alone to most people because modern frames built index directly into collar housing.

Same idea.

Tag:

**BK-9 INDEX TONGUE / RETIRED / RESPONSE UNKNOWN / NO MATCHING FRAME IN LOT**

Auction.

Good question.

I looked again.

Mounting holes.

Mechanical bias.

Could possibly be adapted as repeatable displacement indicator.

Possibly.

"I don't know yet."

Sori smiled.

"Then no."

"Maybe cheap."

"Still no."

"Counterweight pucks useful."

"No."

Ressa grinned.

"Everyone asks."

Seven copper.

Lot 2, chain guides.

Four.

Three.

Eighteen.

Twenty-two.

Twenty-six.

"Still."

Quickly twelve.

Fifteen.

Eighteen.

Technically.

"Yes."

"Yes."

One.

Parts dealer.

Reasonable.

"Three."

Three.

Box probably worth three in metal/components alone.

Could.

Not would.

Fuck auction brain.

Four.

"Four," I said.

Immediately.

There.

Done.

Ressa looked around.

"Six?"

Silence.

She looked at me.

I did nothing.

"Five once. Five twice. Sold."

Like I'd failed.

Harder than it sounded.

Then:

"Good."

"Don't."

"You stopped."

"I had ceiling."

"You had ceiling before bidding?"

"Yes."

She looked genuinely impressed.

Rude.

"Why?"

"Pucks."

"You don't know what you'd use them for."

He stared at me.

"Fuck you."

Excellent.

Auction ended before third bell.

I spent zero copper.

Twenty-five survived.

That should have felt boring.

Lost.

On purpose.

Different skill.

"Good ceiling."

"Probably."

"Probably not."

Outside Dock Eight, Sable Quay was fully awake.

Bells.
