"Deck has benches. Covered middle section. Two stairs to lower washroom. Crew can store crutches during sleep if you want."

"I don't."

"Then don't."

Excellent transport policy.

"Tomorrow deck," I said.

"Three copper."

I paid.

Twenty-five to twenty-two.

Clerk stamped small blue ticket.

**SABLE QUAY -> DUSKPORT**

There.

Choice became object.

Maro bought deck too.

Dask hesitated.

Not money, I thought.

Guild.

"Tomorrow?" I asked.

"Mirror guild opens second bell. Packet fourth."

"You can do both."

He looked relieved.

"Yes."

Bought ticket.

Sori stood at grille.

Clerk said, "Travel?"

She looked at me.

"I hate all of you."

"Three copper," clerk said.

She paid.

Four idiots.

Kel and Vessa stayed Quay.

That changed crew.

Not breakup.

Not drama.

Just people choosing differently.

Good.

We told them outside.

Kel shrugged.

"Bring back something stupid."

"No."

"You will."

"Probably."

Vessa looked at four tickets.

Then at me.

"You're not my crew tomorrow."

That landed.

"I know."

"If something goes wrong, you make your own call."

"I know."

"Don't lock in because you think that's what I'd ask."

There.

Interesting.

"Okay."

She held gaze.

"Greg."

"I heard you."

"Good."

Then she offered hand.

I took it.

No ceremony.

"You were useful," she said.

"High praise."

"It is."

Kel clapped my good shoulder carefully.

"If you come back missing other leg, I'm charging repair labor."

"Fair."

Sori said, "Why is that the standard?"

"He has pattern."

"One is not pattern."

Dask said, "Statistically, sample size is inadequate."

Everyone told him to shut up.

Perfect.

Afternoon opened.

No work.

No auction left.

Ticket in pocket.

Twenty-two copper.

Vale twenty-three.

One copper difference again.

Funny.

I could have paid five for bunk.

Didn't.

Deck was fine.

I could have bought PF-3.

Didn't.

Still maybe wanted it.

That was okay.

Wanting did not create obligation.

Neither did bidding.

Neither did money.

Neither did road.

I spent rest of afternoon doing something radical.

Nothing strategic.

Walked Quay.

Ate fried dough for bits.

Watched crane crew move six barrels without dropping any.

Bought paper and charcoal for bits because I was low.

Sat on river wall.

Tavi's striped rock came out of bag.

I rolled it in palm.

Carrow object.

Duskport ticket beside it.

Two directions.

Not enemies.

I wrote home.

Not full route report.

Cala would hate that.

Short.

**Still safe. Work ended at Sable Quay. I chose to keep going downriver tomorrow with Maro, Sori, and Dask. Duskport, one day and one night by packet. This part is my choice. Shoulder almost normal. Crutch repaired. I have money. I miss you. Tell Tavi his rock is now farther from home than he is. Tell Lyssa I am telling her because I chose something.**

I stopped.

Read last line.

Kept it.

There was public post west at evening bell.

Not fast.

Good enough.

I paid postage in bits.

No copper.

Then sat until sun lowered.

Lume turned gold.

Correct direction.

Respectable river.

Tomorrow I'd ride it thirty miles farther away.

Not because bridge failed.

Not because Survey extended contract.

Not because strange light needed witness.

Not because anyone needed me.

Because I bought ticket.

That was different.

Maybe stupid.

Maybe good.

Usually same ingredients.

Ticket stayed in shirt pocket.

I checked twice.

Then third time because growth had limits.
# CHAPTER 408

## THE MEDIATOR

Dask nearly missed the boat because of mirrors.

Of course he did.

Fourth bell had not rung yet.

It had only threatened to.

But packet crew had already started pulling the last freight net tight when Dask came running down Sable Quay with one hand on his coat, one on a narrow paper tube, and absolutely no dignity.

Sori stood beside me under the covered middle deck.

"Leave him."

"Cruel."

"Educational."

Maro leaned against rail.

"He bought something?"

"If he did, I'm throwing it overboard."

Dask reached gangplank.

Deckhand blocked him with arm.

"Ticket."

Dask bent over, breathing hard.

"Pocket. Left. No, other left."

Deckhand looked at us.

I pointed.

"His left."

Ticket appeared.

Blue.

Stamped.

Valid.

Dask boarded three breaths before gangplank lifted.

Sori said, "You look terrible."

"Guild opened late."

"Did you buy the finder?"

"No."

There.

Growth everywhere.

"What is tube?" I asked.

"Comparative backing samples. Paper only."

Sori narrowed eyes.

"Free?"

"Yes."

"Suspicious."

Packet horn sounded.

Sable Quay began moving backward.

No.

We did.

That remained one of river travel's little lies.

The packet was called **Bright Gull**, painted on stern in blue letters over older red letters someone had failed to sand completely away.

Long low hull.

Two decks.

Cargo middle and forward.

Passenger deck aft and center.

Covered roof over maybe half.

Open benches along rails.

Small galley window.

Lower washroom exactly two stairs down and four more inside, which clerk had technically described without mentioning how narrow everything was.

I managed.

Crutches fit if turned sideways.

Bag stayed under bench between feet.

Quietener wrapped.

WS-F/9 wrapped separately.

Tavi rock in side pocket.

Twenty-two copper.

Vale twenty-three.

No job.

No Vessa.

That last one felt stranger than expected.

Not bad.

Just space where instruction usually lived.

Captain was **Iven Sarr**, woman maybe forty-five, dark hair cut at jaw, scar under lower lip, voice made for being heard through rain.

She gave passenger rules from center deck.

"Three scheduled stops before Duskport. We do not leave channel without cause. We do not wait for private arguments. If you fall overboard, yell before you become difficult to find. Meals cost bits unless ticket says otherwise. Night deck lights out one bell after dark except marked rail lamps. Anyone touching cargo seals will spend rest of trip discussing regret with my mate."

Good captain.

Mate was **Rell Koss**, thin man with enormous mustache and no visible sense of humor.

Probably hidden under mustache.

Passenger mix maybe thirty.

Traders.

Families.

Two soldiers off duty.

A woman with cages of white river birds.

Three apprentices sharing one blanket despite not being cold.

Old man asleep before Quay disappeared.

One child carrying wooden wheel everywhere.

And a woman named **Tessa Morn**.

I noticed her because she wanted something too loudly.

Not at first.

At first she just watched west bank.

Late thirties maybe.

Brown coat too warm for day.

Hair braided tight.

One small leather case under both hands like it might run away.

She asked Rell twice how long to **Mile House Landing**.

He answered both times.

"About three bells."

Second time she asked, "If river's good?"

"If river's river."

Not helpful.

Accurate.

Bright Gull cleared Sable basin by fifth bell.

Quay noise fell behind.

Lower Lume widened.

Banks flatter.

More reed islands.

Channel markers taller and painted in pairs.

Freight barges moved in slow lines downstream.

One carried timber stacked high enough to offend balance.

Dask read paper samples.

Sori pretended not to nap.

Maro watched shore like someone seeing childhood story he had missed.

I enjoyed doing nothing.

For maybe an hour.

Then Tessa Morn began asking everybody.

Not us first.

Crew.

A merchant.

Bird woman.

One soldier.

Rell again.

Finally Sori heard enough to become curious.

Dangerous.

"What's wrong?" she asked.

Tessa looked at her.

Then at our group.

"My son is at Reedbank."

There.

Not Mile House.

Different.

Sori said, "Reedbank isn't scheduled?"

Tessa shook head.

"Private landing. Half mile beyond Mile House on north bank."

Rell, walking past, said without slowing, "We are not stopping there."

Tessa turned.

"You don't know what I'm asking."

"You've asked four crew. I know."

"Then stop."

Rell stopped.

Mustache remained in motion from momentum.

"Captain decides channel deviations. Private landing is outside route."

"It's not outside channel."

"Landing is shallow side cut."

"At this water it isn't."

"You a pilot?"

"I grew up there."

That changed texture.

Rell's face did not.

"Captain decides."

Tessa looked at us like crew had become wall.

Sori said, "What happened to your son?"

Tessa gripped leather case.

"He cut his leg five days ago. Mill blade. Not deep enough to take it. Deep enough to get dirty. Reedbank healer wrote me yesterday. Fever started. I have feverglass and redroot tincture from Sable Quay. If I wait Duskport, then packet back, that's two days. Maybe more."

Human problem.

There it was.

"Why not get off Mile House and go overland?" Maro asked.

"Road washed two weeks ago. Foot path exists. Three miles through reed flats."

She looked at my crutches then away quickly.

"For me, maybe two bells if dry. With case. At night if we arrive late."

"Could hire cart?" Sori asked.

"Mile House has one cart when axle isn't broken. I don't know."

Dask said, "How old is your son?"

"Fourteen."

Tessa's voice changed on number.

Not dramatic.

Worse.

Held.

"His name is Oren."

Nobody asked.

She needed us to know.

Captain Iven eventually came because Rell told her passenger was recruiting opinions.

I liked Rell slightly more for phrasing.

Iven listened.

All of it.

Then said, "No Reedbank stop."

Tessa went white with anger.

"You didn't even look."

"I know Reedbank cut."

"At summer low?"

"At this draft."

"You carry less than full cargo."

"Still too much to promise turn room if north wind pushes stern."

"Then put me in skiff."

That was new.

Iven's jaw tightened.

"Skiff is emergency equipment."

"This is an emergency."

"Not aboard."

There.

Procedure.

Clean line.

Ugly result.

Tessa looked around like she wanted somebody to say what all of us were thinking.

Fourteen-year-old with fever.

Medicine in mother's hands.

Skiff hanging twenty feet away.

"What would make it emergency enough?" she asked.

Iven said nothing for one breath.

Then:

"Aboard emergency. Collision. Person over water. Fire. Hull failure. Medical crisis on packet. Skiff launch into side cut for private delivery risks crew, schedule, passengers, and equipment."

"Schedule."

Tessa spat word.

Iven's eyes hardened.

"Yes. Schedule. There are people aboard with reasons too."

And there it was.

Other half.

Bird woman raised hand slightly.

"My birds have to reach Duskport quarantine before morning inspection. Miss it, I hold them another day and lose contract."

One merchant said, "I have auction papers that close tomorrow second bell."

Soldier near rail said, "My sister's wedding."

Other soldier looked at him.

"You said funeral."

"Wedding feels longer."

Not helping.

A thin man in gray coat stood from bench near stern.

"My daughter is being sentenced tomorrow."

Silence.

There.

He had not spoken all morning.

"Appeal hearing," he corrected. "If I am late, she goes without family witness."

Tessa stared at him.

He stared back.

Neither apologized.

Good.

Because neither should.

Iven said, "Mile House is scheduled. We reach before dusk. Anyone leaving there accepts own onward travel. Reedbank is not scheduled."

Tessa said, "So correct procedure is my son waits because your skiff belongs to emergencies that happen on your deck."

Iven's face changed slightly.

Not because accusation false.

Because it was true enough to hurt.

"Correct procedure keeps thirty passengers and crew from making every private emergency the packet's emergency," she said.

Also true.

Fuck.

Everyone looked uncomfortable.

I was not involved.

Beautiful.

Then Tessa looked at me.

Of course.

"You were Survey?"

Road gossip.

Maybe crutches.

Maybe Sori records case.

"For a while."

"You know routes. Risk."

"Some."

"Tell her."

No.

Absolutely not.

"Tell her what?"

"That half mile isn't going to kill thirty people."

There.

She wanted a claim.

Not truth.

A weapon shaped like truth.

My normal skill finally became problem.

I could not bound that into clean answer because I did not know Reedbank cut, boat draft, wind, current, skiff handling, captain's liability, Oren's fever severity, Mile House cart status, path condition, or how much delay mattered to everyone else.

Correct thing was say I didn't know.

I did.

"I don't know enough to tell her that."

Tessa flinched like I had struck her.

"Of course."

There.

Procedural honesty.

Human cost.

I hated feeling of it.

She stood.

"Everybody on this boat knows how to explain why they can't help."

Then walked forward.

Sori watched her go.

"That was fair."

"I know."

"Also not fair."

"I know."

Maro said, "Both can happen."

Dask looked miserable.

Good.

He had no instrument for this.

Neither did I.

For next half bell, nothing happened.

Which meant everybody thought about it.

Worse.

I went to captain.

Not to tell her what to do.

Iven stood near wheelhouse with route slate.

"You're here to argue?"

"Maybe ask."

"Ask."

"What's actual Reedbank risk?"

She studied me.

"You believe her?"

"I believe she has medicine and wants to get it to son. I don't know fever."

"Good answer."

"Annoying."

"Useful."

Vessa would like her.

"Actual risk?"

Iven pointed river chart.

"Main channel here. Mile House dock south bend. Reedbank cut enters north side after bend. Bright Gull can enter mouth if water holds. Turning inside is problem. We would need back out or continue shallow loop that rejoins main river two miles later."

"Can skiff do it?"

"Yes."

"Then why hard no?"

She looked at me long enough.

"Because launching skiff needs two crew. Skiff returns maybe half bell, maybe bell if landing bad. Packet drifts or anchors. We miss Gate Nine traffic slot."

"How much delay?"

"Could be one bell. Could be three. Gate Nine after dark can hold us until morning depending freight priority."

There.

Not fifteen minutes.

"So thin man's appeal?"

"Potentially missed. Bird quarantine definitely. Auction likely."

"Could Tessa ride skiff and skiff continue to Reedbank then not return?"

"Emergency skiff isn't passenger taxi and Reedbank has no packet-certified return crew."

"Could one crew stay?"

"Then I'm short one trained hand overnight through Gate Nine."

All bad.

"Could another boat take her from Mile House?"

"Maybe."

"Maybe meaning?"

"Local fishers sometimes run Reedbank. No guarantee."

"Can we know before Mile House?"

Iven paused.

There.

Question.

Not answer.

"Signal tower at Mile House can see private-dock flag board if clear."

"Does Reedbank have flag?"

"Yes."

"Can Mile House signal ahead to see if boat is available?"

"They can ask."

"Can we ask now?"

Iven looked upriver toward next relay post.

"At Marker Seventy-two. Fifteen minutes."

There.

Not solution.

Information.

My favorite drug.

But user wanted human problem, not procedure magically fixing it.

So I asked next.

"If no local boat?"

"Then she's at Mile House with foot path. Or I break route."

"Would you?"

Iven looked at passengers behind us.

"I don't know."

There.

Captain finally had no clean answer either.

Good.

Bad.

We reached Marker Seventy-two.

Iven signaled tower.

Flags went up.

Questions relayed.

Mile House answered ten minutes later.

No cart.

Axle broken.

Of course.

Private boat?

One Reedbank fisher at Mile House currently.

Good.

Boat leaving north before dusk.

Better.

Capacity?

Two passengers plus light bag.

There.

Answer.

Almost too clean.

Then final flag.

Fisher would not take north cut after sunset because channel stake missing near Willow Tooth.

Bright Gull expected Mile House about half bell before sunset if no delays.

Window tight.

If packet lost twenty minutes, Tessa misses fisher.

And river already had freight queue ahead.

Human problem remained.

Iven told Tessa.

Hope made her worse.

"Then don't lose twenty minutes."

Iven said, "I'll do my job."

"Your job keeps getting between me and mine."

"My job is carrying you there alive and on published route."

"My son is already there alive. Maybe."

There.

Knife.

Iven turned away because captain could not afford reply.

Freight queue appeared around next bend.

Three barges.

One timber raft.

Gate-control tug moving upstream.

Bright Gull slowed.

Tessa stood at rail counting minutes without clock.

Everyone felt it.

Bird woman too.

Gray-coat father too.

Nobody became villain.

That was worse.

Dask asked me quietly, "Can packet overtake?"

"Ask captain."

He did not.

Good.

We lost twelve minutes.

Maybe fourteen.

Tessa started crying without sound.

Just tears.

I looked away.

Then freight tug signaled our lane open earlier than expected.

Bright Gull moved.

Not fast.

Packets didn't become racehorses because mother cried.

But Iven took every legal opening.

I could tell because Rell changed deck rhythm.

Lines ready before turns.

Cargo checks early.

Meal service delayed.

No one announced favor.

They just worked.

That mattered.

Mile House dock came into view with sun low.

Small stone landing.

Three houses.

Signal tower.

One broken cart visibly missing wheel.

And a narrow fishing skiff tied outside pier.

Tessa made sound.

Not word.

Relief breaking.

Bright Gull docked.

Fisher was **Noll Renn**.

Of course.

Dask started.

Noll held up hand.

"No."

Dask looked wounded.

Tessa barely heard any of it.

She was down gangplank before Rell finished saying wait.

Iven snapped, "Passenger Morn!"

Tessa froze.

Captain walked to rail.

"Your ticket continues Duskport. If you leave here, packet owes no onward transport."

"I know."

"Reedbank fisher says north cut dark unsafe after sunset. You have maybe half bell."

"I know."

"If he refuses midway, you do not order him through."

Tessa looked at captain.

Anger still there.

Gratitude too.

Neither canceled other.

"I know."

Iven nodded.

Tessa looked at me.

I expected thanks.

She said, "You could've helped sooner."

There.

Good.

Because she was right from her side.

"Maybe."

She shook head.

"You people love maybe."

Then left.

Noll shoved off with Tessa and medicine case.

Skiff angled north.

We watched until reeds swallowed them.

No confirmation.

No success yet.

No clean closure.

Bright Gull departed on schedule plus some minutes.

Bird woman still had chance at quarantine.

Gray-coat father still had chance at hearing.

Tessa had chance at son.

Captain had not broken route.

Procedurally, excellent.

Emotionally, nobody felt excellent.

Sori sat beside me after dark.

Deck lamps low.

River black.

Dask and Maro somewhere forward buying soup.

"You found workaround," she said.

"Captain did."

"You asked question."

"That's not same as helping."

"Tessa thinks so."

"She thinks I should've made captain stop."

"Would you?"

I looked at river.

There.

Question.

All options hurt somebody.

If I had authority and no fisher existed.

Stop and maybe cost father hearing.

Bird woman's contract.

Crew safety.

Thirty people schedule.

Or don't stop and maybe cost boy leg.

Maybe life.

No clean answer.

"I don't know," I said.

Sori nodded.

Not disappointed.

That helped less than expected.

"You usually know what not to claim," she said.

"Yes."

"Different problem."

"Yes."

"Eventually you have to choose anyway."

There.

Fuck.

She went for soup.

I stayed.

Bright Gull moved downriver.

Somewhere behind us, Tessa was trying to reach Oren before dark.

Somewhere ahead, gray-coat man was counting distance to daughter's hearing.

Bird woman checked cages for fourth time.

Captain watched channel.

Everybody wanted something badly.

River did not care.

Procedure cared only enough to keep system from becoming thirty private wars.

Necessary.

Insufficient.

That was new.

I had spent months learning not to pretend uncertainty was certainty.

Useful skill.

Not enough skill.

Sometimes facts narrowed choices until all remaining choices were cruel in different directions.

Then somebody still had to choose.

No Vessa tomorrow to say which.

No captain for every problem.

No protocol that could carry blame away.

I looked at dark water and felt Duskport pulling east.

Chosen road.

Apparently choice included this too.

Shit.
# CHAPTER 409

## THE COMPANION

Sleeping on packet deck was less romantic than traveling stories implied.

Mostly because traveling stories cut the benches.

And the snoring.

And the child who had been kicking the same wall for twenty minutes.

Not hard.

Just enough.

Tap.

Tap.

Tap.

Sori opened one eye.

"I will throw him into river."

"You don't mean that."

"I mean adjacent to river."

"Better."

Maro had somehow folded himself into corner bench and looked asleep.

Dask was not asleep.

Of course.

He sat under covered middle deck with guild pamphlet open against one knee and lantern hooded low.

I said, "If you blind yourself before Duskport, I'm not reading signs for you."

"This is not bright."

"It's brighter than closed eyes."

"Most things are."

There.

Packet wisdom.

Bright Gull moved through dark water with steady engine thrum under floorboards and occasional chain-rattle from cargo restraint.

Banks had become shapes.

A few lamps.

Black reeds.

Farmhouses rare now.

More docks.

More industrial lights.

Lower Lume smelled different.

Wider water.

Mud flatter.

Smoke farther away but more constant.

I lay on bench with shoulder bag under head because trusting thirty strangers with twenty-two copper and several weird tools felt optimistic.

Crutches rested against chest and rail.

Not comfortable.

Secure.

Good enough.

Tessa's seat was empty.

That was annoying.

Not because I wanted her back.

Because empty seats made absences visible.

Her medicine case had gone with her.

Good.

Oren maybe got it.

Maybe didn't.

No way to know tonight.

I hated not knowing less than I hated pretending.

Progress.

Still hated it.

Somewhere near first night bell, packet slowed.

Not stop.

Just changed rhythm.

Passengers noticed because everyone notices when thing carrying them changes mind.

Rell Koss came through covered deck.

"Gate Nine queue. Twenty minutes if honest. Forty if not. Stay aboard. Galley open."

Gray-coat father stood immediately.

The one with daughter's hearing.

He had name now because Sori had asked earlier.

**Harven Coil.**

Mid-fifties.

Gray coat too warm for weather.

Hands that kept folding and unfolding same handkerchief.

"Forty?"

Rell looked at him.

"Could be less."

"Could be more."

"Yes."

Harven's jaw worked.

"You said Duskport morning."

"Captain said morning or midday if river and traffic cooperate."

"My daughter's hearing is second bell."

"I know."

"Do you?"

Rell did not take bait.

"Yes."

Harven looked past him toward forward deck.

"Can we pass?"

"Not without slot."

"Can you buy priority?"

There.

Interesting.

Rell's face changed one degree.

"Sometimes."

"Then buy it."

"Packet doesn't carry discretionary gate-priority budget."

Harven laughed once.

Not humor.

"Of course."

Then bird trader stood.

Her name was **Mira Sol**.

She had three reed cages under cargo awning, each holding long-necked gray birds that looked personally offended by existence.

"Do not buy priority," she said.

Harven turned.

"Excuse me?"

"If packet pays emergency rate, captain will pass cost to manifest surcharge. I have twelve birds under commercial ticket and quarantine fee already paid."

"My daughter may be sentenced tomorrow."

"And my birds may be refused if inspection closes before arrival."

"They're birds."

Mira went still.

Bad choice.

Harven knew it after saying it.

Too late.

"They are six months of breeding," Mira said. "And contract deposit. And my sister's farm debt."

"I didn't mean..."

"You meant exactly enough."

There.

Human problem again.

Apparently river had curriculum.

Sori sat up fully.

Dask closed pamphlet.

Maro opened eyes without moving head.

Rell said, "No gate priority purchase tonight. Captain's decision."

Harven looked toward forward stairs.

"Then I want to speak to her."

"She is navigating queue."

"I don't care."

"She does."

Rell moved on.

Harven followed three steps, stopped because crewman blocked forward access politely and completely.

Then he turned back.

Looked at me.

Of course.

Why did everyone keep deciding I had face for this?

"You helped that woman."

I stayed on bench.

"A little."

"Help me."

Sori looked at ceiling.

I said, "With what?"

"Tell captain to buy priority."

There it was.

Again.

Same shape.

Different people.

I could say I didn't know enough.

True.

Useful maybe.

Also starting to sound like shield.

"How much is priority?" I asked.

Harven blinked.

"I don't know."

"Then first question."

Mira said, "Gate Nine after-hours priority isn't fixed. Depends freight queue."

Harven turned on her.

"You know?"

"I ship birds."

"Then help."

She laughed without warmth.

"You called them birds."

"They are birds."

"And she is your daughter. Both can be true while you remain an ass."

Maro coughed into sleeve.

Not hiding laugh well.

Harven rubbed face.

"Fine. I'm sorry."

Mira looked surprised.

So was I.

"Fine," she said.

Not forgiven.

Enough.

Sori said, "What actually happens if you miss second bell?"

Harven sat opposite us.

That was first time he looked old instead of angry.

"Hearing starts second bell. Appeals clerk said family witness statement can be accepted before decision if I am present. If I'm not, counsel can read written statement."

"You have written statement?"

"Yes."

"Then your daughter isn't unrepresented."

"No."

"But you want to be there."

He looked at her.

"She's nineteen."

There.

Not answer.

All answer.

Sori nodded.

Mira's face softened despite herself.

Harven continued.

"She hit a dock foreman."

Dask said, "Why?"

Sori elbowed him.

Harven didn't mind.

"Foreman grabbed her apprentice by throat. She broke his nose. He fell. Hit edge. Lost two teeth. Foreman says assault. Yard says insubordination. Apprentice says foreman started it. Three workers say they didn't see."

There.

Mess.

"What is she appealing?" I asked.

"Work-ban order and six months labor levy."

"Not prison?"

"No."

Some tension left room.

Harven saw it.

"That still destroys her trade."

"I know."

"Do you?"

He stopped himself.

"Sorry."

Mira said, "Learning."

He ignored her.

Sori asked, "What does your being there change?"

Harven looked down at handkerchief.

"Maybe nothing."

There.

He laughed once.

"That's the worst part. Maybe nothing. But if she looks up and I'm not there..."

He did not finish.

That was wanting something badly.

Not legal leverage.

Presence.

Hard to price.

Hard to procedure.

Mira said, quieter, "My inspection closes third bell, not second."

Harven looked at her.

"So?"

"So if priority costs too much, don't buy it for me."

That was not same as consent.

Not quite.

She stared at cages.

"But if delay goes past first bell, I need to know. I can send runner from first dock if we arrive south quay. Quarantine office might hold clerk if warned. Maybe."

There.

Another maybe.

But hers.

Harven said, "Thank you."

Mira shrugged.

"Still birds."

One bird hissed.

"See?" she said. "Assholes."

Humanity restored.

I got up.

Shoulder fine.

Right hand fine.

Crutches planted against moving deck without much thought now.

"I'm going to ask gate cost."

Sori looked at me.

"Captain said no priority."

"I'm not asking her to buy."

"Good."

There.

Different problem.

Facts still useful.

Just not verdict.

Rell was near aft rail watching signal lamps.

I asked, "Priority cost?"

"Why?"

"Because people are arguing about thing with no number."

He considered.

"Fair."

Forward signal tower showed three red lamps and one amber.

Gate structure ahead looked like black wall with lit slots.

Rell said, "Current after-hours pass for packet our class likely two to four copper. Could spike six if stone convoy keeps slot."

"Per packet?"

"Yes."

"Who pays if captain chooses?"

"Company account if operational need. Passenger-originated discretionary priority gets surcharge by manifest class."

"Meaning?"

"Split across eligible tickets. Freight heavier share. Passenger lighter."

"How light?"

"Depends final cost. Maybe bit or two each passenger. Freight account takes most."

There.

Small individually.

Not nothing commercially.

"Why captain refused?"

Rell looked at me.

"Because if every personal deadline buys gate slot, packet timetable becomes auction. Also company reviews discretionary passes. Too many and captain loses route."

There.

Another person with something to lose.

Captain's job.

Not just budget.

I nodded.

"Can passengers voluntarily cover priority without forcing others?"

Rell's mustache moved.

"Technically? Maybe."

"Allowed?"

"Private payment to gate office can be accepted if packet master approves and payment doesn't alter freight contract."

"Would Iven approve?"

"Ask her."

"She's navigating."

"Yes."

Fair.

Rell looked forward.

"Queue just moved. Might be irrelevant in five minutes."

Of course.

We waited.

Five minutes became eight.

No move.

Harven came aft.

"Well?"

"Two to four copper likely, maybe six. Passenger surcharge usually small because freight carries most. Captain also risks route review if she uses discretionary priority too often."

Harven stared.

"I'll pay six."

Mira had followed.

"You have six?"

"Yes."

"Then pay it yourself."

"I said I would."

"You said buy priority."

"Fine. I will pay."

Sori arrived behind them.

"Hold."

Harven's face tightened.

"What now?"

"Can you pay six and still afford Duskport transport, hearing fees, food?"

He looked angry again.

Then tired.

"Barely."

"Barely is answer."

"I don't care."

"Your daughter might."

"She can yell at me after."

There.

Decision.

Maybe bad.

His.

I said, "Captain still has to approve."

Harven looked at me.

"Then ask her."

I did.

Not because I knew right answer.

Because he had one.

Iven met us at stair after another ten minutes when queue stabilized enough to spare attention.

Harven spoke first.

"I will personally pay up to six copper for discretionary priority if Gate Nine accepts it. No passenger surcharge. No freight surcharge."

Iven looked at him.

Then me.

"This your idea?"

"Question was mine. Choice is his."

Good sentence.

Keep.

She looked back at Harven.

"You understand priority does not guarantee hearing arrival. We can still be delayed downstream."

"Yes."

"You understand payment may be nonrefundable once gate slot changes."

"Yes."

"You understand I can still refuse if passage unsafe or traffic command says no."

"Yes."

Mira said, "And if he pays, my birds don't become reason."

Iven looked at her.

"Correct."

Harven said, "Fine."

Iven considered longer than comfortable.

Then shook head.

"No."

Harven went white.

"Why?"

"Stone convoy is emergency bank repair material. Priority would move us ahead of it if accepted now. Gate office already flagged convoy. I'm not asking them."

There.

Fuck.

Correct procedure had found another person not even aboard.

Somewhere downstream bank needed stone.

Delay that and who knew what happened.

Harven laughed.

"Of course."

Not at her.

At world.

Iven said, "Queue estimate now seventeen minutes. We hold."

"And if it becomes forty?"

"Then we reassess."

"My daughter..."

"I know."

Harven snapped.

"Stop saying that."

Iven did.

Good.

Nobody won.

Seventeen minutes became nineteen.

Then gate lamp went green.

Bright Gull moved.

No bought priority.

No heroic exception.

Harven sat with face in hands until gate doors closed behind us.

Mira put cup of tea beside him without speaking.

He drank it.

People were irritating.

Also good.

Night deepened after Gate Nine.

Some passengers finally slept.

I didn't immediately.

Sori sat beside me on rail bench.

"You asked different question."

"Apparently still didn't fix it."

"That's point."

"Annoying point."

"Yes."

Harven's decision had been clear.

Pay six.

Captain's decision had been clear.

Don't delay emergency bank stone.

Both could be right enough.

One still lost.

Maybe only nineteen minutes.

Maybe those nineteen mattered.

Maybe downstream delays erased everything anyway.

Could not know.

Sori said, "You keep trying to find option where nobody has to be villain."

"Usually exists."

"Does it?"

I thought of first life.

War.

Triage.

Retreats.

Contracts.

People left behind.

Orders that saved hundred and killed ten.

Of course it didn't always exist.

I had known that.

Maybe second life had let me forget because smaller problems usually had smaller exits.

"No," I said.

"Good."

"Why is admitting misery good?"

"Because otherwise you'll keep treating it like missing information."

There.

She was annoying when correct.

"Sometimes it is missing information."

"Yes."

"Sometimes better question changes options."

"Yes."

"And sometimes every option still sucks."

"Congratulations."

"I hate this lesson."

"Good lessons usually rude."

Maro spoke from bench across aisle.

Eyes closed.

"Bad lessons too."

Sori looked over.

"Were you awake?"

"Unfortunately."

Dask said from floor near cargo wall, "I was also awake."

"Nobody asked."

"I know."

Progress.

Eventually I slept.

Not well.

Packet sleeping came in pieces.

Engine vibration.

Cold rail against shoulder.

Someone stepping around crutch tip.

A baby crying once then stopping.

Bird hissing in dream.

At some point river widened enough that packet movement changed.

Less bank echo.

More open-water roll.

I woke before dawn.

Maro was already awake.

Of course.

He stood at rail with cup.

"Duskport?" I asked.

"Not yet."

East ahead was gray.

Lower Lume had broadened into something almost lake-like between low banks.

Freight silhouettes moved in distance.

Tall masts.

Long barges.

A line of lights far downstream that could have been town or industrial docks.

Maybe both.

Harven stood forward near passenger boundary.

Still awake too.

I joined him.

He didn't look at me.

"How late are we?"

"Rell says maybe twelve minutes off schedule now."

"Could make it."

"Yes."

He nodded.

Then:

"I shouldn't have said birds."

"Probably not."

"I don't care about birds."

"I know."

He looked at me sharply.

I almost apologized for phrase.

Then didn't.

"That's problem," he said. "Everyone cares about one thing most. Then boat acts like all things weigh same."

There.

"Boat has to carry all of them," I said.

"I know."

He smiled without humor.

"See?"

Fair.

We stood quiet.

After a while he said, "If I miss hearing, she'll know I tried."

"Probably."

"You people love probably too?"

"Deeply."

That got tiny laugh.

Good.

Not forgiveness.

Not needed.

When physical sun began lifting east, river reflected it correctly.

No wrong dawn.

Nobody cared.

Good.

For once light could just be light.

Then packet horn sounded twice.

Rell walked deck.

"Duskport outer basin in one bell. South quay first. North quay after. Passengers with hearings, inspections, and other reasons to ruin my morning should gather bags now."

Harven moved immediately.

Mira too.

They looked at each other.

Harven said, "Quarantine third bell?"

"Yes."

"If we dock south first, your office north?"

"East quarantine pier."

He thought.

"I know court runner near south gate. If I make hearing, I can send boy east with arrival notice."

Mira stared.

"Why?"

"Because they're birds."

She looked offended.

Then laughed.

"Asshole."

"Apparently."

There.

People disagreeing did not mean people stayed enemies.

Useful.

Bright Gull rounded long mud point.

Duskport appeared.

Not as city all at once.

First cranes.

Then towers.

Then roofs stacked behind water.

Then ships.

Actual ships.

Not river packets.

Deep-hulled coastal vessels moored beyond lower quays.

Masts like stripped forest.

Warehouses five stories high.

Smoke stacks.

Temple roof with green tiles.

A market canopy running nearly quarter mile along water.

And farther east, beyond basin mouth, something gray-blue and enormous.

Sea.

I stopped breathing for one second.

Not because never seen sea.

First life had.

Because second life had not.

Carrow felt impossibly inland suddenly.

Sori came beside me.

"Your face."

"Shut up."

"That's sea."

"I know."

"You look surprised."

"I am allowed."

Dask pushed between us.

"Duskport mirror district is near east quay."

We both looked at him.

"What?"

Maro laughed.

Bright Gull sounded horn again.

South quay workers waved signal flags.

Harven held handkerchief so tightly knuckles went white.

Mira checked bird cage straps.

Everyone wanted something.

Duskport didn't care.

Good city already.

I had twenty-two copper.

A debt.

A bag of tools.

Three companions who had chosen same boat for different reasons.

A home west.

An unknown boy behind us with fever.

A father beside me trying to reach daughter before second bell.

A bird trader trying not to lose farm contract.

And sea ahead.

Adventure, apparently, was not one big problem.

It was thirty small lives all insisting theirs mattered most.

Hard to argue with any of them.
# CHAPTER 410

## THE PROSPECT

Duskport had stairs.

Of course it did.

The sea had apparently not improved civilization.

Bright Gull tied south quay eight minutes before second bell.

Harven Coil was standing before gangplank touched stone.

Captain Iven pointed at him.

"You fall in, hearing gets worse."

"Understood."

"Wait."

He waited.

Barely.

Mira Sol had both bird cages ready.

One bird made noise like old hinge.

"Shut up," she told it.

It did not.

Rell Koss got freight lane clear.

Gangplank down.

Harven went first after crew.

Not running.

Fast enough to make running jealous.

Mira followed with porter and cages.

At bottom Harven turned.

"Quarantine runner. South gate?"

"Blue arch," Mira said.

"I remember."

"You better."

Then he disappeared into Duskport.

No ending.

Good.

Or terrible.

Same thing sometimes.

Mira looked at me before leaving.

"If you want word about the boy, packet office posts notices from upriver."

"Good to know."

Fucking face had traveled thirty miles and developed reputation.

Then she left.

Iven stood by rail while passengers emptied.

I offered hand.

"Thanks."

"For what?"

"Not killing us."

"Low standard."

"Reliable one."

She shook once.

"Duskport packet office is Pier Four if you need westbound. Bright Gull returns tomorrow afternoon unless freight changes."

There.

Return route.

I liked knowing.

Didn't mean taking.

Maro came down behind me.

Dask had already stopped halfway down gangplank because he could see something reflective across basin.

Sori shoved him gently between shoulders.

"Move."

"Those are signal mirrors."

"Move while knowing that."

We entered Duskport.

First thing city did was almost run me over with fish.

Cart.

Fish cart.

Important distinction.

Driver yelled.

I moved.

Current body could move fast enough for fish.

Progress.

South quay was not a street.

It was six streets arguing over same stone.

Porters.

Carts.

Rope sellers.

Customs runners.

Fishmongers.

Sailors carrying things that should have required three sailors.

Children with message tubes.

Three languages in first hundred yards, one I knew poorly, one not at all.

Salt on everything.

Not river salt.

Sea.

I could smell it under tar and fish and smoke.

I wanted to go see water.

Dask wanted mirrors.

Sori wanted lodging before we became four idiots paying emergency rates after dark.

Maro wanted food.

Democracy failed immediately.

Sori won.

"Beds first."

"Sea is large," Maro said. "Will probably remain."

"Probably?" Dask asked.

Maro looked at him.

"For Greg."

I hated all of them.

Cheap lodging near south quay existed if cheap meant relative to Duskport.

First place wanted two copper each.

No.

Second wanted one copper plus bits, shared loft, wash basin extra.

Maybe.

Third had sign:

**ANCHOR'S END**

**BEDS 1C**

**FLOOR 4 BITS**

**NO FIGHTING INSIDE**

Inside.

Important qualifier.

Sori inspected loft.

I inspected stairs.

Twelve.

Wide.

Rail both sides.

Acceptable.

Innkeeper **Pell Varo** looked at crutches.

"Loft bed near stair?"

"Yes."

"Same price."

"Good."

"If you fall, scream after landing. Wakes fewer people."

"Thoughtful."

We took four beds.

I paid one copper.

Twenty-two to twenty-one.

There.

Vale twenty-three.

Back under debt by two.

Still fine.

Bag locked in foot chest with my small brass lock.

Quietener.

WS-F/9.

Tavi rock.

All there.

Crutches stayed with me.

Obviously.

Then sea.

We walked west through market lane because Dask said mirror district was west and Sori said if he vanished alone she would sell his coat.

"You cannot."

"I can sell coat."

"It's mine."

"Market decides."

Duskport widened as we moved.

River basin on right.

Warehouses gave way to chandlers and workshops.

Then shipyards.

Masts everywhere.

Not decorative.

Working forest.

Ropes thicker than wrist.

Anchor chains.

Sails stretched for repair across frames like giant skins.

Magic lived here too.

Not fireworks.

Blue seam-lines along one drydock wall that pushed seep water toward drains.

Wind vanes with tiny charged fins correcting dock cranes.

A warehouse door whose iron threshold flashed dull green when sealed cargo crossed.

Dask pointed at all of it.

I told him to conserve finger.

Then we reached seawall.

There.

Ocean.

No river bank opposite.

No far wall.

Gray-blue under pale morning.

Coastal ships small against it.

First-life me knew oceans.

Second-life me stood on two crutches and looked anyway.

Body did not care what memory knew.

Chest opened a little.

Wind hit face.

Salt.

Gulls.

Distance.

Maro stood beside me.

"Worth three copper?"

"Yes."

Sori said, "Don't tell packet office."

Dask was looking backward.

Of course.

"There's a mobility shop."

I turned.

Across seawall road, between sailmaker and rope-repair yard, hung wooden sign shaped like boot.

Except boot ended at shin.

Under it:

**HARK & VENN**

**BRACES / ARTICULATED SUPPORTS / WORK LIMBS / MARINE FITTINGS**

I looked longer than intended.

Sori noticed.

Of course.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"That's a lie."

Maro read sign.

Then looked at left leg.

Not rude.

Direct.

"Have you ever tried one?"

"Work limb?"

"Peg."

There.

Word.

Simple.

I looked down.

Left knee.

Nothing below.

Crutches had become normal enough I sometimes forgot they were equipment until city gave me twelve stairs and fish cart.

"Not current life."

Sori frowned.

"You had one first life?"

"No. Had leg."

"Right."

Maro said, "Could help."

I knew.

Obviously.

But knowing abstractly and shop existing across street were different things.

Dask said, "Depends socket, stump tolerance, alignment, terrain, gait training, whether knee control is good, whether they use passive foot or rigid end, weight, load transfer, skin shear, and probably six other things I don't know."

Sori stared.

"That was almost useful."

"I read."

"Terrifying."

I looked at shop again.

A man came out carrying wooden lower leg.

Not pirate peg.

More complex.

Leather socket above.

Shaped shin.

Broad split foot with dark rubber-like sole.

Brass side stay.

He handed it to woman in dock-worker trousers.

She sat on bench, rolled trouser leg, fitted it over right below-knee stump, tightened straps, stood between parallel rails outside shop.

Then walked.

Not perfectly.

Better than crutches for carrying crate with both hands.

That mattered.

Very much.

I had two hands.

Crutches usually rented both.

Peg could buy one or both back depending task.

Mobility not replacement.

Option.

Options were expensive.

Sori said, "Go ask."

"We just got here."

"Shop is here now."

"I can ask later."

"You can."

She paused.

"You won't."

Rude.

Maybe true.

Maro said, "Ask price. Doesn't buy it."

Auction lesson returned.

Wanting did not create obligation.

Neither asking.

Fine.

We crossed.

Hark & Venn smelled like leather, cedar shavings, oil, and hot metal.

Walls held braces.

Splints.

Work hooks.

Artificial feet.

Jointed knees for above-knee loss.

Rigid pegs.

Marine legs with wide soles and drainage holes.

Some beautiful.

Some ugly.

All practical.

Woman behind bench looked up.

Maybe sixty.

Dark skin.

White hair cut short.

Three fingers missing from left hand.

She looked at me once.

Not crutches first.

Gait.

Shoulders.

Left knee.

Hands.

Then crutch tips.

Professional.

"Below knee."

"Yes."

"How long?"

"Current body?"

She paused.

"Interesting answer."

Sori covered face.

"Long enough healed," I said.

"Pain?"

"Not usually."

"Skin breakdown?"

"No."

"Knee range?"

I flexed.

She watched.

"Good. Sit."

"I'm only asking."

"Then sit while asking."

I sat.

Her name, according brass plate:

**MASTA VENN - LIMBWRIGHT**

Venn.

No.

I did not ask.

Growth.

She pulled stool.

"What do you want?"

There.

Not what happened.

What do you want.

I looked at doorway.

Dock worker outside walking rails.

"More hands."

Masta nodded.

"Good answer."

"Not speed."

"Speed comes later if it comes."

"I want to carry something without using mouth."

"Also good."

Sori said, "He does use mouth."

"Sometimes."

Masta ignored her.

"You travel?"

"Apparently."

"Work?"

"Mixed. Field. Theatre. Carrying. Survey recently."

"Fight?"

I looked at crutch tooth repair.

She followed eyes.

"Yes," I said.

"Don't fight on first fitting."

"Wasn't plan."

"People say that."

She asked permission before touching knee/stump.

I said yes.

Quick assessment.

No drama.

Pressure points.

Scar position.

Knee control.

Hip strength.

Standing balance between rails.

She had me put crutches aside and stand on right leg with hands on rails.

Then shift pelvis left into padded temporary support block under stump without loading full.

Body understood possibility immediately.

Not walking.

Just line.

Weight could go somewhere that was not right foot or hands.

Interesting.

Very.

Masta stepped back.

"You could use work leg."

Sori leaned forward.

"How much?"

I glared.

Masta did not.

"Depends."

Of course.

"Basic rigid dock peg, leather socket, no articulated ankle, indoor/flat-yard use, three fittings and gait rail sessions. Eighty-four copper if wood ordinary and no rush."

Silence.

Dask said, "Oh."

Good contribution.

Masta continued.

"Travel work limb with split foot, replaceable sole, better wet grip, side stay, adjustable socket because bodies change. One silver and eighteen copper."

There.

Silver.

Actual silver.

No conversion stated.

Did not need one.

More than twenty-one copper.

Much more.

"Marine drainage foot and salt-resistant fittings starts one silver thirty-six. Articulated ankle higher. Charged balance assist higher than that. I don't recommend charged assist first limb unless you enjoy paying me to watch you fall creatively."

I liked her.

Hated prices.

"How much higher?" Dask asked.

Masta looked at him.

"Are you buying?"

"No."

"Then enough."

Sori smiled.

I asked, "Basic peg would help carrying."

"Yes. Also teach bad gait if you pretend it's travel leg. Flat work. Short durations first. Skin checks. You keep crutches."

"Travel one?"

"Better for what you're describing. Still keep crutches. Limb is tool, not miracle. Some days stump says no. Some ground says no. Some stairs say go fuck yourself."

There.

Perfect.

"Timeline?"

"If I take you."

I blinked.

"If?"

"I have eleven active fittings. Three shipyard injuries this month. Two children outgrowing braces. One sailor who keeps breaking same foot because he believes instructions are personal attack."

"Fair."

"Deposit gets slot."

"How much?"

"Travel leg, twenty copper deposit. Balance due before final hardware leaves shop. Fittings over maybe eight to twelve days if you're local and stump behaves. Longer if not."

Twenty.

I had twenty-one.

Technically could place deposit.

Then one copper.

Food.

Lodging.

Travel.

Vale.

No.

Not impossible.

Worse.

Possible enough to hurt.

Sori knew arithmetic.

Her face changed.

No teasing.

"You could reserve it," she said.

"And have one copper."

"Yes."

"No."

Masta nodded.

"Good."

I looked at her.

"You don't want deposit?"

"I want clients who can eat between fittings."

There.

Again.

Human being.

"Any cheaper used?"

"Sockets are body-specific. Feet and stays sometimes reused. I have two salvage feet. Neither fits your load well. Could make something cheaper and worse. Won't."

"Payment plan?"

"For locals with guild guarantor. You're not local."

"Work trade?"

Masta looked at me again.

Different.

"What work?"

Good question.

I had no answer ready.

"Depends what you need."

"I need money."

"Same."

Maro coughed laugh.

Masta leaned back.

"You said Survey."

"Temporary regional route crew. Glasswake prep, field observation, load work, records."

"Records?"

"Yes."

"Mechanical?"

"Some."

"You know load frames?"

"Enough to be dangerous if unsupervised."

"Better answer than expert."

She tapped bench with three-fingered hand.

"My brother runs **Venn Marine Recovery** on East Hook. Salvage diving, wreck lift, quay recovery. They lost condition clerk two weeks ago. Not dead. Married someone in Gullhaven and left with no notice, which my brother considers worse."

Dask said, "Condition clerk?"

"Recovered hardware gets logged before yard tears it apart. Salt exposure. Charge residue. deformation. ownership marks. whether object should be touched. whether object should be left in fucking bucket until someone qualified arrives."

I looked at her.

She looked at me.

There.

"Pay?"

"Ask him."

"Would it cover leg?"

"Not in afternoon."

"Few days?"

"Depends whether you're useful."

Good.

"Name?"

"Hark Venn."

I looked at shop sign.

Hark & Venn.

"You're Venn."

"Yes."

"He's Hark?"

"No. Hark died twelve years ago. My brother is also Venn. Shop name stayed because changing sign costs money."

Sori laughed.

Masta pointed at her.

"You understand business."

"Unfortunately."

I asked, "You'd refer me?"

"I said ask him. Referral is expensive word."

"Fair."

"Tell him Masta said you know enough to answer questions without pretending. He'll hate that less than most things."

That was not referral.

It was something.

I looked at travel leg hanging wall.

One silver eighteen copper.

No.

Not yet.

But now price existed.

Worker existed.

Work existed.

Path existed.

Different from wanting impossible thing.

Dangerous.

"If I earn enough, you can make me one that actually fits how I move? Not generic dock peg."

Masta's expression sharpened.

"If you do fittings. If you listen. If you stop when skin says stop. If you don't ask me to build weapon because you fought dogs once."

"How did you know about dogs?"

"You have repaired bite marks on crutch and face of man waiting to tell story."

Fuck face.

"Then yes," she said. "I can build you work leg. Maybe travel leg. We find out what body tolerates before we decide what ego wants."

There.

I wanted it.

Badly.

Not because title.

Not because pirate joke.

Because I had spent nineteen years of second life adapting around missing lower leg and months making crutches into extensions of hands.

I was good on them.

Very good.

That did not mean I had to stay on them forever.

A peg would not give leg back.

It would give option.

Hands.

Standing.

Carrying.

Different fights maybe.

Different work.

Different city grammar.

Stairs still assholes.

But fewer things rented both arms.

Twenty-one copper in purse.

One silver eighteen copper on wall.

I did not know exact conversion here.

Didn't matter.

Not enough.

For first time in a while, that felt useful.

Not enough meant target.

Sori saw it happen.

"Oh no."

"What?"

"You have work face."

"Apparently I have many faces."

"This one's worse."

Maro said, "East Hook?"

Masta pointed through back wall.

"Follow seawall east past drydock bells. Big red recovery crane. Yard sign missing R because storm. Says VEN MARINE RECOVE Y. Can't miss it."

Dask said, "That seems missable."

"Then get lost."

We left.

Sea still there.

Duskport still huge.

Mirror district still waiting for Dask.

Harven's daughter somewhere in court.

Mira's birds somewhere in quarantine line.

Tessa's son upriver with fever, maybe.

World did not reorganize around my leg.

Good.

But my day did.

I stood on seawall with both crutches under arms and looked east.

Red recovery crane visible above roofs.

Missing-letter sign probably below it.

Twenty-one copper.

One silver eighteen.

No job.

Maybe job.

I could go sightseeing.

Could shop.

Could spend day at sea.

Could turn west tomorrow.

Instead I adjusted shoulder bag.

"East Hook," I said.

Sori groaned.

"You just arrived."

"Yes."

"You were supposed to wander."

"I am wandering toward employment."

"That's not wandering."

Maro started walking.

"Depends how bad interview goes."

Dask looked west toward mirrors.

Then east toward us.

Pain.

Actual pain.

"Go," Sori told him. "Mirror guild. Meet Anchor's End tonight."

"You're sure?"

"Yes."

He vanished west.

Three of us went east.

I looked once more at shop sign behind us.

Work limbs.

Not miracle.

Tool.

Expensive tool.

Good.

I knew what to do with expensive.

Become worth more.
